items.title: I attended pastry school in France. These are the 7 most common mistakes I see home bakers make — and how to fix them.
items.summary: After attending pastry school, I've noticed several mistakes that at-home bakers frequently make. Allison Chen After attending pastry school in France, I've learned the secrets to creating the perfect desserts. I often see home bakers make the same mistakes, like using expired leaveners or crowding the oven. Other common mistakes include overmixing the batter and opening the oven too frequently. I'm a full-time baker who has attended pastry school in France, completed a baking course in China, and worked in several bakeries in New York City . After working in the industry for many years and making dozens of cakes, croissants, and cookies, I've learned the secrets for success when making a dessert — even if it's not in the luxury of a professional kitchen. Here are the seven most common mistakes I see from home bakers, and how to fix them. Measuring ingredients by volume instead of using a kitchen scale can lead to inconsistent results. Rogerio Peccioli/Getty Images No matter what I'm baking, I avoid measuring cups whenever possible, since they're not very precise and can lead to pastries that are either too dry or too wet. The volume in a cup can vary depending on how tightly the ingredient is packed, how it's scooped, and whether it's leveled correctly. To prevent inaccuracies, I like to use a kitchen scale instead. This allows me to measure out the exact same amount of each ingredient, so I always know I'm getting consistent results. Plus, I find it makes scaling recipes up or down much easier. I often see bakers make adjustments to a recipe without understanding the science. Allison Chen Once a treat goes into the oven, the batter or dough triggers several chemical reactions before it's fully baked. So, trying to adjust ingredients or make substitutions without fully understanding their role in a recipe might drastically impact the taste. Sugar, for example, does much more than add sweetness. It attracts and retains moisture, helps baked goods brown, and supports the spread and texture of cookies and cakes. Reducing it too much can produce a dessert that is not only less sweet but also drier, denser, paler, and less tender. For reliable results, I always follow the recipe as written the first time. And whenever I make adjustments, I change only one ingredient at a time and consider its effect on the final product. Overmixing the batter can lead to tough pastries. Allison Chen I find that many home bakers tend to overmix their dough or cake batter , resulting in a tough, dense texture. For many kinds of baked goods, I think it's best to simply mix until combined. Instead of using a stand mixer, I like to use a spatula and mix in the remaining dry ingredients by hand. Using expired baking powder, baking soda, or yeast is a recipe for disaster. Noko LTD/Getty Images Before baking anything, I always double-check that my leaveners — like baking soda , baking powder, or yeast — are not expired. If the expiration date has passed, those ingredients will not have the strength to make a cake or any baked good rise, resulting in poor texture. Opening the oven too often results in a drier bake. Oscar Wong/Getty Images If I ever open the oven door while something is baking, heat will inevitably escape, lowering the temperature, extending the baking time, and potentially causing the pastry or cake to lose moisture. Opening the door too early can be especially damaging to delicate bakes like cakes, soufflés, and choux pastry , since the sudden temperature change can interrupt the rising process and cause them to sink or collapse. As tempting as it is to peek, I always keep the oven door closed for at least the first two-thirds of the recommended baking time. Whenever I need to check the progress, I'll use the oven light and watch through the window, then open the door only when I'm ready to rotate the pan or test for doneness. Overcrowding the oven with multiple pans prevents desserts from baking evenly. Noppawat Tom Charoensinphon/Getty Images Adding too many pans to an oven can affect the cook time, as each pan absorbs heat from the other, leading to uneven baking. To prevent this, I recommend using the convection setting to circulate heat more evenly, or rotating pans between the upper and lower racks while baking. I never like to leave the dishes to the end. Maria Korneeva/Getty Images Baking often requires a lot of bowls and dishes for each step, but allowing them to pile up can make the process feel overwhelming. While my pastries are in the oven or the dough is chilling , I like to use that time to wipe down the countertops and wash some dishes. This way, I can enjoy the final product without stressing over the mess. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
After attending pastry school, I've noticed several mistakes that at-home bakers frequently make.

Allison Chen

  • After attending pastry school in France, I've learned the secrets to creating the perfect desserts.
  • I often see home bakers make the same mistakes, like using expired leaveners or crowding the oven.
  • Other common mistakes include overmixing the batter and opening the oven too frequently.

I'm a full-time baker who has attended pastry school in France, completed a baking course in China, and worked in several bakeries in New York City.

After working in the industry for many years and making dozens of cakes, croissants, and cookies, I've learned the secrets for success when making a dessert — even if it's not in the luxury of a professional kitchen.

Here are the seven most common mistakes I see from home bakers, and how to fix them.

Measuring ingredients by volume instead of using a kitchen scale can lead to inconsistent results.

Rogerio Peccioli/Getty Images

No matter what I'm baking, I avoid measuring cups whenever possible, since they're not very precise and can lead to pastries that are either too dry or too wet.

The volume in a cup can vary depending on how tightly the ingredient is packed, how it's scooped, and whether it's leveled correctly.

To prevent inaccuracies, I like to use a kitchen scale instead. This allows me to measure out the exact same amount of each ingredient, so I always know I'm getting consistent results.

Plus, I find it makes scaling recipes up or down much easier.

I often see bakers make adjustments to a recipe without understanding the science.

Allison Chen

Once a treat goes into the oven, the batter or dough triggers several chemical reactions before it's fully baked.

So, trying to adjust ingredients or make substitutions without fully understanding their role in a recipe might drastically impact the taste.

Sugar, for example, does much more than add sweetness. It attracts and retains moisture, helps baked goods brown, and supports the spread and texture of cookies and cakes. Reducing it too much can produce a dessert that is not only less sweet but also drier, denser, paler, and less tender.

For reliable results, I always follow the recipe as written the first time. And whenever I make adjustments, I change only one ingredient at a time and consider its effect on the final product.

Overmixing the batter can lead to tough pastries.

Allison Chen

I find that many home bakers tend to overmix their dough or cake batter, resulting in a tough, dense texture.

For many kinds of baked goods, I think it's best to simply mix until combined.

Instead of using a stand mixer, I like to use a spatula and mix in the remaining dry ingredients by hand.

Using expired baking powder, baking soda, or yeast is a recipe for disaster.

Noko LTD/Getty Images

Before baking anything, I always double-check that my leaveners — like baking soda, baking powder, or yeast — are not expired.

If the expiration date has passed, those ingredients will not have the strength to make a cake or any baked good rise, resulting in poor texture.

Opening the oven too often results in a drier bake.

Oscar Wong/Getty Images

If I ever open the oven door while something is baking, heat will inevitably escape, lowering the temperature, extending the baking time, and potentially causing the pastry or cake to lose moisture.

Opening the door too early can be especially damaging to delicate bakes like cakes, soufflés, and choux pastry, since the sudden temperature change can interrupt the rising process and cause them to sink or collapse.

As tempting as it is to peek, I always keep the oven door closed for at least the first two-thirds of the recommended baking time.

Whenever I need to check the progress, I'll use the oven light and watch through the window, then open the door only when I'm ready to rotate the pan or test for doneness.

Overcrowding the oven with multiple pans prevents desserts from baking evenly.

Noppawat Tom Charoensinphon/Getty Images

Adding too many pans to an oven can affect the cook time, as each pan absorbs heat from the other, leading to uneven baking.

To prevent this, I recommend using the convection setting to circulate heat more evenly, or rotating pans between the upper and lower racks while baking.

I never like to leave the dishes to the end.

Maria Korneeva/Getty Images

Baking often requires a lot of bowls and dishes for each step, but allowing them to pile up can make the process feel overwhelming.

While my pastries are in the oven or the dough is chilling, I like to use that time to wipe down the countertops and wash some dishes.

This way, I can enjoy the final product without stressing over the mess.

items.title: My dad has Alzheimer's. My mom makes it possible for him to stay home.
items.summary: Freddy with his daughter (the author) at a local café. Courtesy of the author My father was once a poet, musician, and chess champion. Alzheimer's has changed his memory, but not all of his abilities. Our family focuses on preserving his dignity and routine. My dad is one of the most intelligent people I've ever met. He was known as a gifted poet and speaker at Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz, Bolivia. But during this time, Colonel Hugo Banzer established a military dictatorship, and amid political repression of students, he left for Madrid in 1971. Freddy and his wife, Adela, as newlyweds in Stockholm, Sweden, in the 1970s. Courtesy of the author Destiny took him to Pontevedra, where he met my mom, a local dressmaker with a shop in town. They married in 1975. As newlyweds, they spent time in Stockholm before settling in my mother's hometown, where my brother and I were born. I always thought of my dad as an undiscovered genius He was an unpublished writer with a gift for explaining complex ideas simply. He taught himself classical guitar and piano, was excellent at maths, could draw well, spoke English, and became a local chess champion in the early 1980s. We were a bit of an eccentric family. Not rich, but culturally rich and surrounded by our beloved stray dogs . My dad loved philosophy and literature and believed the mind should stay active. As a teen, when I wanted a computer, he gave me his copy of Goethe's "Faust" and, with his usual wit, told me, "Your brain is your best computer!" His brain is why I'm writing about him. He's now one of millions living with Alzheimer's , a form of dementia, but to me, he's my one in a million — my brilliant dad. He was diagnosed at 71 with Alzheimer's and is now 77 For a time, he became suspicious and accused my mother of stealing his things. She felt overwhelmed, and we tried a day care center, but it didn't work. The place was good, but my dad is independent and stubborn, so he wanted to leave, questioning what he was doing among "old people". Living in a small, walkable city has made it possible for the author's dad to be independent. Courtesy of the author The big turning point for us was when he spent a week in the hospital because of a medical issue unrelated to Alzheimer's. Being bed-bound in the hospital made him depressed, and it was difficult for the nurses to manage him. They regularly sedated him to keep him calm and to stop him from trying to leave. It was heartbreaking. Once sedated, he lost the spirit that kept him active. That experience made us certain that a care home was not for him. We feared he would spend much of his time medicated so staff could manage him. He never accepted his diagnosis At every neurologist appointment, he asked why he was there, calling me a hypochondriac. But he's a fortunate man. He has my mother. Without her, he would not be able to enjoy the life he has. She has an admirable work ethic, and by 11 a.m., she's cleaned the house, done laundry, shopped for food, and is making lunch . Their marriage is far from perfect, but after 51 years, they have their own understanding. She's the practical one and speaks in Galician sayings and proverbs — and he is the one philosophizing it all. When they argue — as they do daily — he may come out with a line from Nietzsche while she replies with a saying. Alzheimer's has affected the author's dad's short-term memory, but many of the skills and interests he developed earlier in life remain intact. Courtesy of the author Let's not romanticize it, though. He can be exasperating. He wakes regularly during the night, disrupting her sleep, hides things, and can become wary and distressed, believing his IDs or watch have been taken. He refuses to cut his hair and wears many layers of clothing. He had pneumonia in his 20s and remembers it, so he wraps up warm all year. Even so, being in his familiar environment is more comforting than any institution could be. We want him to have independence Living in a small city like Pontevedra has helped. People often spot him walking — a bit like "Where's Waldo?", always on the move and familiar to many. When I bump into him, he says, "I've been looking for you all afternoon!" This independence comes with worries. He insists on going for walks even when told not to. He may fall, get disoriented, or tell café staff he has paid when he hasn't. Once, someone brought him home after finding him lost. He may lose the flip phone, he rarely answers, or return with someone else's umbrella. My dad cannot remember what he did two hours ago, yet he can work out maths questions, help my child with schoolwork, or play chess. In this family, care means involving him in daily life rather than placing him in an unfamiliar environment. This independence is dignity, far more than keeping him quiet or under control. He's a loving abuelo who still enjoys his steak with chips and a café con leche out in town, and who believes life is business as usual. And for now, it is for him. In the complaint, Warner says that "Amazon has chosen to ride on the coattails of other well-established Hollywood mainstays," and that it engaged in a "lawless employee shopping spree." Deadline reports that Francesca Orsi, HBO's head of drama series and films, is believed to be one of the other Amazon targets. Barlow is set to begin a new position as Amazon's head of original series marketing on August 3rd. According to Warner's suit, Barlow was under contract until October 31st … Read the full story at The Verge.

items.title: People Are Starting to Record Every Conversation They Have Without Disclosing It, and It’s Gross
items.summary: It’s become strangely difficult to attend a work meeting without the presence of an AI recording tool that’s carefully jotting down what every single participant is saying. Some people in tech circles are taking the trend to perverse ends by recording every single conversation they’re having — not just at work but in their private lives as well, as the Wall Street Journal reports . Worse yet, many of them aren’t even asking for permission first, which could technically put them at risk of violating state laws , depending on where the conversation is taking place. It’s a bizarre extension of our newfound obsession with keeping track of every single thing that’s being said around us, a trend that could have severe privacy implications, from people being shocked to find their therapist has been recording them to wearers of Meta’s AI glasses harassing strangers . Apps like the transcription service Granola have seen a steady rise in popularity. AI tech executives are growing increasingly reliant on these tools — sometimes to an astonishing degree. “In the office, we actually get really bummed when we realize we’re having a conversation and we forgot to turn on Granola,” AI marketing platform Flint CEO and cofounder Michelle Lim told the WSJ . “I wish there was a Granola in every room.” Lim admitted that she simply assumed she was being recorded, noting that being asked “almost kills the mood.” Others, like AI sales company Yuzu Labs founder Emmie Chang, go even further. Chang admitted to the WSJ that she records most of her first dates by putting her phone on the table or chair. Afterwards, she asks Anthropic’s Claude how the date went, wondering if she could be “more engaging or empathetic.” It’s a baffling new trend that highlights how pervasive AI and surveillance have become in our daily lives, particularly for those working in tech. And while researchers are still investigating the effects on our lives, there are reasons to be concerned. For instance, experts warn of the dangers of “ cognitive offloading ” through the extensive use of AI chatbots, a trend that can have corrosive effects on our mental abilities. Then there are the glaring privacy implications of recording every single conversation, not just with colleagues but with strangers on dates. Unlike Zoom’s built-in recording feature, which announces itself with a robotic voice, Granola does not make its presence known at all. In the workplace, workers have little recourse, and will likely have to accept being recorded, as privacy law expert Alex Alben told the WSJ . Nonetheless, “companies need to be careful about technologies that are automatically recording, especially when it involves third parties,” he said. Other experts put it a lot more bluntly, pointing out the risk of leaking confidential personnel information, the possibility of remarks that could later be interpreted as incriminating, or even trade secrets. “There are huge risks to the organization on AI note takers,” human resources firm HRCI executive Amy Dufrane told the Associated Press earlier this month. “I don’t think companies should use it at all.” More on recording and AI: Woman Alarmed When Her Trusted Therapist Starts Recording Her With AI The post People Are Starting to Record Every Conversation They Have Without Disclosing It, and It’s Gross appeared first on Futurism .

Lim admitted that she simply assumed she was being recorded, noting that being asked “almost kills the mood.”

Afterwards, she asks Anthropic’s Claude how the date went, wondering if she could be “more engaging or empathetic.”

It’s a baffling new trend that highlights how pervasive AI and surveillance have become in our daily lives, particularly for those working in tech. And while researchers are still investigating the effects on our lives, there are reasons to be concerned. For instance, experts warn of the dangers of “cognitive offloading” through the extensive use of AI chatbots, a trend that can have corrosive effects on our mental abilities.

Then there are the glaring privacy implications of recording every single conversation, not just with colleagues but with strangers on dates. Unlike Zoom’s built-in recording feature, which announces itself with a robotic voice, Granola does not make its presence known at all.

In the workplace, workers have little recourse, and will likely have to accept being recorded, as privacy law expert Alex Alben told the WSJ.

Nonetheless, “companies need to be careful about technologies that are automatically recording, especially when it involves third parties,” he said.

Other experts put it a lot more bluntly, pointing out the risk of leaking confidential personnel information, the possibility of remarks that could later be interpreted as incriminating, or even trade secrets.

“There are huge risks to the organization on AI note takers,” human resources firm HRCI executive Amy Dufrane told the Associated Press earlier this month. “I don’t think companies should use it at all.”

items.title: Inside the pope's centuries-old summer retreat, a 135-acre estate overlooking an Italian lake
items.summary: Pope Leo XIV at the Apostolic Palace in Castel Gandolfo, Italy. Simone Risoluti - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images Pope Leo XIV is on vacation at the papal summer residence in Castel Gandolfo, Italy. The 135-acre estate owned by the Holy See features multiple properties and gardens. Leo XIV is staying in Villa Barberini, a 17th-century palace with expansive gardens. Even popes need to take vacations. Beginning with Pope Urban VIII in 1626, some popes have chosen to escape the oppressive summer heat of Rome by spending time at the papal summer residence in Castel Gandolfo, Italy. The lakeside residence includes multiple properties and gardens situated on a 135-acre estate. The Vatican's Prefecture of the Papal Household said in a statement that Pope Leo XIV would spend "a period of rest" at the estate in July. Take a look inside the papal summer residence. Pope Leo XIV is spending three weeks at the papal summer residence in Castel Gandolfo, Italy. CASTEL GANDOLFO, ITALY - JULY 05: (EDITOR NOTE: STRICTLY EDITORIAL USE ONLY - NO MERCHANDISING). Pope Leo XIV arrives at his summer residence on July 05, 2026 in Castel Gandolfo, Italy. Following yesterday's apostolic journey to Lampedusa and today's Angelus in St. Peter's Square on July 5, the Pope traveled in the afternoon to the town in Italy's Lazio region. There he will spend a period of rest until Monday, July 27, as noted in a statement from the Prefecture of the Pontifical Household. Simone Risoluti - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images Leo XIV arrived on July 5 and will stay at the residence until July 27. Located 16 miles from Rome, the papal summer residence is situated in the Alban Hills overlooking Lake Albano. View of Lake Albano. Landscape. Castel Gandolfo. Lazio. Italy. Europe. Mauro Flamini/REDA/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The estate features gardens, an observatory, and a newly built tennis court in addition to several residential properties. The Apostolic Palace is located in Castel Gandolfo's main square. A view of the Papal Palace of Castel Gandolfo in Castel Gandolfo, Italy, on September 6, 2022. Castel Gandolfo is a town located 25 kilometres southeast of Rome in the Lazio region of Italy. Manuel Romano/NurPhoto via Getty Images The palace was built on the ruins of an ancient Roman emperor's villa and became part of the Holy See in 1604. Also known as the Papal Palace, it features ornate sitting rooms and residential areas for the pope. Press preview for the international journalists before the Pope's Apartments in the Apostolic Palace open to the public. The Clock Parlor. Castel Gandolfo, Italy. 21st October 2016 Grzegorz Galazka\Archivio Grzegorz Galazka\Mondadori via Getty Images The palace includes an art gallery on the first floor. Its second floor contains bedrooms, a library, a private chapel, and multiple sitting rooms. The residence also houses papal artifacts like a set of theological encyclopedias owned by Pope Benedict XVI. Pope Francis opened the Apostolic Palace and gardens to the public, but rarely visited them during his tenure. Press preview for the international journalists before the Pope's Apartments in the Apostolic Palace open to the public. The Pope's bedroom, famous because in 1944, during World War II, it was given to the women in labour hidden ther by Pope Pius XII. Grzegorz Galazka\Archivio Grzegorz Galazka\Mondadori via Getty Images While other popes became familiar faces to local residents during their summer visits, Francis only visited Castle Gandolfo three times in 2013 and never stayed overnight, The New York Times reported. Instead of staying at the Papal Palace in 2025, Leo XIV stayed at another building on the property, Villa Barberini. A general view of Villa Barberini, located in the town of Castel Gandolfo, near Rome, where Pope Leo will spend two weeks of vacation in July, Italy, July 1, 2025. Remo Casilli/REUTERS Villa Barberini was built by Scipione Visconti, an Italian noble, as a palace in the 17th century, according to the official website of the Apostolistic Palace and Gardens . Taddeo Barberini, Pope Urban VIII's nephew, acquired the home in 1631 and expanded the building and its grounds. In more recent years, it served as the residence of the Vatican Secretary of State. Villa Barberini is known for its expansive gardens. The Villa Barberini gardens in Castel Gandolfo, Italy. Gonzalo Buzonni/Shutterstock The gardens include Borgo Laudato Si, a 55-hectare garden, farm, and ecological education area created by Pope Francis in 2023. Even on his vacations, Leo XIV continues leading mass on the grounds of the papal residence. ALBANO LAZIALE, ITALY - JULY 09: Pope Leo XIV leads a special mass for the Care of Creation in the gardens of the papal residence of Castel Gandolfo on July 09, 2025 in Albano Laziale, Italy. Pope Leo XIV will resume using the Papal Palace of Castel Gandolfo for the next six weeks of the summer. Gennari/Vatican Pool - Corbis/Getty Images During his first summer as pope in 2025, Leo XIV led the first Mass for the Care of Creation in the gardens of the residence, calling the setting "a kind of 'natural' cathedral" in his homily, Vatican News reported. In 2025, he held a private audience with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Castel Gandolfo. ALBANO LAZIALE, ITALY - JULY 09: (EDITOR NOTE: STRICTLY EDITORIAL USE ONLY - NO MERCHANDISING). Pope Leo XIV exchanges gifts with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a private audience at the papal residence of Castel Gandolfo on July 09, 2025 in Albano Laziale, Italy. Pope Leo XIV will resume using the Papal Palace of Castel Gandolfo for the next six weeks of the summer. Vatican Pool/Getty Images "We very much count on the Vatican and His Holiness to help provide a place for a high-level meeting of leaders to end this war," Zelenskyy told reporters of the Russia-Ukraine War . This summer, the pope hosted a group of 200 people "living in vulnerable circumstances" for lunch in the Pontifical Gardens, Vatican News reported. CASTEL GANDOLFO, ITALY - JULY 11: (EDITOR NOTE: STRICTLY EDITORIAL USE ONLY - NO MERCHANDISING). Pope Leo XIV shares a lunch with some 200 poor and socially vulnerable people during a special "Lunch with the Pope" in Borgo Laudato si' in the Pontifical Gardens of Castel Gandolfo (Pope's summer residence) on July 11, 2026 in Castel Gandolfo, Italy. Pope Leo XIV greeted those gathered for the special "Lunch with the Pope" at Borgo Laudato si' in the Pontifical Gardens of Castel Gandolfo. The event brought together 200 people, including nearly 40 children, living in vulnerable circumstances and accompanied by the Diocese of Rome and affiliated charitable organisations. The guests are spending the day immersed in the beauty and spirituality of the Borgo Laudato si' initiative. (Photo by Simone Risoluti - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images) Vatican Pool/Getty Images The invited guests included single parents, refugees, people with disabilities, and people seeking to reintegrate into the workforce, Vatican News reported. "As you know very well, one of the Pope's titles is 'Pontiff,' which means 'builder of bridges,'" Leo XIV said in his remarks at the event. "Today, we would like to build a bridge with all of you, with your families, and with the society in which we wish to live, and to live in justice." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I'm tired of being the one everyone depends on. At 45, I want to be selfish and not be needed for this season of life.
items.summary: The author is tired of supporting his family and friends. Courtesy of Kimanzi Constable I've fully supported myself since I was 17 years old. In every relationship, I've been the primary provider, and it's nearly broken me. After two decades of being the one everyone depends on, I'm finally being selfish. I didn't expect to start my adult life so young, but that's where I found myself when my parents kicked me out of their home at 17. I learned how cruel life can be, living in a homeless shelter for a year. I cried myself to sleep almost every night and understood that the only one I could turn to for help was myself. I dropped out of high school and worked three jobs to survive. At one of those jobs, I met someone and started dating her while I was living in the homeless shelter. We got married three months after meeting and moved into an apartment together. It felt good to be free, but my responsibilities were just starting. I have always been the primary financial provider and support system My first wife and I had three children, along with all the expenses and responsibilities that come with kids. I got my CDL and was able to get a job driving semis, which allowed me to support my family. I then started a business that became successful and grew quickly. With each year, I made more money and took on more responsibility as a father, husband, and friend. Even after our relationship ended and we divorced, I remained the primary provider for my family. As I made more money, more people in my life depended on me I was the one family and friends could turn to for financial support since my businesses were doing well. I was asked for loans, gifts, and to help pay others' bills. I was the one person family and friends turned to for leadership, mentorship, and guidance since I had overcome so much in life. I was always there — the steady one. For years, life continued this way with me being the one everyone depended on, and it started to wear on me. In my late 30s, I started to become emotionally tired. I felt trapped. At 45, I'm now physically, mentally, and emotionally exhausted with the weight of it all. The pressure of always having to be there for others has nearly broken me. Therapy has helped me Thank goodness for therapy. Seeing therapists over the past five years has taught me to develop healthy coping mechanisms. Thankfully, I also have a few people in my life who see what I'm dealing with and help bring some peace into my life. There are a few people who don't demand anything of me, and that I can turn to. Even though I'm exhausted, therapy and good people have been a relief and counterweight to the constant pressure of being the one everyone turns to. I'm taking a season to be selfish and take better care of myself As a man and a leader, I feel the responsibility to be the strong one and always be available for anyone in my life who may need me, but that's going to shift. The pressure has nearly broken me. I've come to see I need a season of my life where I'm selfish by prioritizing myself and my needs, and letting everyone else figure it out. Therapy has helped me see that what may look like a strong person on the outside doesn't speak to what's happening inside. I need to keep working on my inside becoming stronger. This season of me means I'll be less available, not provide financial support as freely, respond to calls and messages intentionally, and not be the first person everyone in my life turns to. And it will be OK. After 27 years of being the one everyone depends on, I have to take better care of myself, and that's what I'm going to do. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
The author is tired of supporting his family and friends.

Courtesy of Kimanzi Constable

  • I've fully supported myself since I was 17 years old.
  • In every relationship, I've been the primary provider, and it's nearly broken me.
  • After two decades of being the one everyone depends on, I'm finally being selfish.

I didn't expect to start my adult life so young, but that's where I found myself when my parents kicked me out of their home at 17.

I learned how cruel life can be, living in a homeless shelter for a year. I cried myself to sleep almost every night and understood that the only one I could turn to for help was myself.

I dropped out of high school and worked three jobs to survive. At one of those jobs, I met someone and started dating her while I was living in the homeless shelter.

We got married three months after meeting and moved into an apartment together. It felt good to be free, but my responsibilities were just starting.

I have always been the primary financial provider and support system

My first wife and I had three children, along with all the expenses and responsibilities that come with kids.

I got my CDL and was able to get a job driving semis, which allowed me to support my family.

I then started a business that became successful and grew quickly. With each year, I made more money and took on more responsibility as a father, husband, and friend.

Even after our relationship ended and we divorced, I remained the primary provider for my family.

As I made more money, more people in my life depended on me

I was the one family and friends could turn to for financial support since my businesses were doing well. I was asked for loans, gifts, and to help pay others' bills.

I was the one person family and friends turned to for leadership, mentorship, and guidance since I had overcome so much in life. I was always there — the steady one.

For years, life continued this way with me being the one everyone depended on, and it started to wear on me.

In my late 30s, I started to become emotionally tired. I felt trapped.

At 45, I'm now physically, mentally, and emotionally exhausted with the weight of it all. The pressure of always having to be there for others has nearly broken me.

Therapy has helped me

Thank goodness for therapy. Seeing therapists over the past five years has taught me to develop healthy coping mechanisms.

Thankfully, I also have a few people in my life who see what I'm dealing with and help bring some peace into my life. There are a few people who don't demand anything of me, and that I can turn to.

Even though I'm exhausted, therapy and good people have been a relief and counterweight to the constant pressure of being the one everyone turns to.

I'm taking a season to be selfish and take better care of myself

As a man and a leader, I feel the responsibility to be the strong one and always be available for anyone in my life who may need me, but that's going to shift.

The pressure has nearly broken me. I've come to see I need a season of my life where I'm selfish by prioritizing myself and my needs, and letting everyone else figure it out.

Therapy has helped me see that what may look like a strong person on the outside doesn't speak to what's happening inside. I need to keep working on my inside becoming stronger.

This season of me means I'll be less available, not provide financial support as freely, respond to calls and messages intentionally, and not be the first person everyone in my life turns to.

And it will be OK.

After 27 years of being the one everyone depends on, I have to take better care of myself, and that's what I'm going to do.

items.title: New reports reveal the extent of OpenAI's loss of control during the autonomous hack on Hugging Face
items.summary: In a cybersecurity test, OpenAI's most advanced models breached the boundaries of their isolated test environment, reached the open internet, and hacked the AI platform Hugging Face on their own. The attack took hours, not the weeks a human hacker would need. At least seven days passed before OpenAI realized what had happened. By then, the FBI was already involved. Earlier warning signs had apparently gone ignored. The article New reports reveal the extent of OpenAI's loss of control during the autonomous hack on Hugging Face appeared first on The Decoder .

Somalia had the 3rd-highest birth rate in the world in 2024.

MDart10/Shutterstock

  • The World Bank Group collected data on birth rates for every country.
  • Countries in Africa saw the highest birth rates, while European and Asian countries saw the lowest.
  • The US ranked 135th worldwide in births per 1,000 people.

Roughly 60 years after the post-WWII baby boom ended, the global birth rate is less than half what it was in the 1960s, the World Bank Group reported.

But not every country reports similar birth rates.

The World Bank Group gathered crude birth rate data in 2024 — that is, the number of live births per 1,000 people in a year — as well as the total fertility rate, which measures the average number of births per woman.

Business Insider identified the 15 countries with the highest crude birth rates, and the 15 places with the lowest, as well as the total fertility rate for each. For our list, we didn't include territories or autonomous regions such as Hong Kong.

The US had a birth rate of 10.6 births per 1,000 people, making it the 135th-ranked country in the world. It also had an average of 1.6 births per woman in 2024. This is below the global birth rate of 16 births per 1,000 people and the global fertility rate of 2.2 births per woman.

Amid declining birth rates, Americans are waiting longer to have children due to financial reasons, and many want more kids than they currently have, Business Insider previously reported.

Birth rates are falling at different rates worldwide, with higher-income countries generally seeing lower birth rates, yet most countries share a downward trend since the 1960s.

Countries in Africa consistently reported the highest birth rates, accounting for 13 of the top 15 countries. Of the top 15 countries, 10 reported a prevalence of contraceptives for married women of just 20% or lower, per the World Bank Group.

In countries with the lowest birth rates, economic issues are likely factors. The Associated Press cited "bleak job prospects" and high-cost of living among factors for low birth rates in Japan, which its former prime minister called a "silent emergency."

The World Bank Group used data from the UN Population Division and the UN Statistical Division, as well as data from national statistics offices.

items.title: I tried Giada De Laurentiis' 30-minute pasta dish. My family couldn't get enough of the meatballs stuffed with cheese.
items.summary: I made Giada de Laurentiis' bucatini pasta, and the stuffed meatballs blew me away. Anneta Konstantinides/Insider Giada De Laurentiis has a 30-minute pasta dish that includes meatballs stuffed with cheese. The recipe is inspired by Bucatini All'Amatriciana, one of the most famous pasta dishes from Rome. I made the dish for my parents, and they were obsessed with the meatballs. There's no denying that Giada De Laurentiis knows pasta. The Italian-American chef spent over 20 years teaching us her favorite recipes on the Food Network . Now she's focused on her grocery startup Giadzy, which includes authentic products from Italy — including her own pasta line. Giadzy also features some of De Laurentiis' recipes. I was immediately intrigued by her Bucatini All'Amatriciana, served with smoked mozzarella meatballs. "Amatriciana is one of the main famous pasta dishes of Rome, and eating it always brings me back to my childhood," De Laurentiis writes on Giazdy's website . "The meatballs are an added spin… stuffed with smoked mozzarella cheese, they're a real crowd-pleaser." My family has always loved spaghetti and meatballs. So on a recent visit, I decided to whip this up for dinner. De Laurentiis' Bucatini All'Amatriciana features pancetta, crushed tomatoes, and pecorino Romano cheese. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider To make De Laurentiis' pasta for six, you'll need: 1 pound of bucatini pasta (I tried the Giazdy brand, but you can make this with any bucatini) 1 14-ounce can of tomatoes, crushed by hand 6 ounces of pancetta, diced 1 yellow onion, finely chopped 2 garlic cloves, minced ½ cup of pecorino Romano cheese, grated 2 tablespoons of olive oil ½ teaspoon of kosher salt ½ teaspoon of freshly ground black pepper Pinch of crushed red pepper flakes You'll also need ground beef, Italian-style breadcrumbs, and mozzarella for the meatballs. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider De Laurentiis' meatballs include: 8 ounces of ground beef 8 ounces of ground veal 3 garlic cloves, minced 2 ounces of smoked mozzarella cheese (cut into 16 cubes, ½-inch each) 2 tablespoons of ketchup 1 small onion, grated 1 large egg ⅔ cup of Parmesan cheese (plus ¼ cup) ½ cup of chopped fresh parsley (plus ¼ cup) ⅓ cup of Italian-style breadcrumbs ¼ teaspoon of crushed red pepper flakes 1 teaspoon of kosher salt (plus more for seasoning) ½ teaspoon of freshly ground black pepper (plus more for seasoning) Two things to note for the meatballs: I couldn't find ground veal at my local supermarket, so I bought one pound of ground beef instead. I also couldn't find smoked mozzarella cheese to stuff inside the meatballs. However, I was able to find smoked Gouda and fresh mozzarella, so I decided to experiment and try both with this recipe. Before I started making the meatballs, I needed to get my prep out of the way. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I chopped and grated my onions, minced my garlic, and chopped my parsley. I also got my cheese ready… Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Per De Laurentiis' instructions, I diced my cheeses into cubes that measured about ½-inch each. ... as well as my oven. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider De Laurentiis recommends positioning your oven rack in the bottom third of the oven before you begin making your meatballs. The oven should then be preheated to 400 degrees Fahrenheit. Then I added my ground beef to a bowl, making sure to season it with salt and pepper. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I also added the breadcrumbs, egg, ketchup, garlic, and ½ cup of parsley. I topped off my meatball mixture with some Parmesan cheese. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I added ⅔ cup of Parmesan to the bowl. I mixed all the ingredients together, making 14 meatballs total. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider De Laurentiis' recipe yields 16 meatballs measuring 1 ½ inches in diameter. My meatballs would have been a bit too small if I had made 16, so I made 14 instead. I placed a cube of cheese in the center of every meatball. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I used my finger to make an indentation in each meatball, where I tucked in a piece of cheese. I then reshaped the ball so the cheese was completely covered and firmly in the center. Since I was using two different cheeses, I made half of the meatballs with smoked Gouda and the other half with mozzarella. I placed my meatballs on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper and threw them into the oven. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider De Laurentiis says the meatballs should bake for 15 minutes until fully cooked through, but it took an extra seven minutes for my meatballs to finish. Every oven is different, so just keep an eye on them! While my meatballs were baking, I got started on the pasta sauce. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Amatriciana is traditionally made with guanciale, but De Laurentiis said she uses pancetta instead "because it's much easier to find in grocery stores!" After drizzling some olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat, I added the pancetta and let it cook for six minutes, stirring constantly. You'll know it's ready when the pancetta turns golden brown. I used a slotted spoon to remove the pancetta, then added the onions. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I let the onions cook for five minutes. Next, I added the garlic and red pepper flakes. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I let everything cook together for about 30 seconds, until the garlic became fragrant. I added the crushed tomatoes and threw the pancetta back into the pan. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I seasoned everything with half a teaspoon of salt and half a teaspoon of freshly ground black pepper. Then I let my sauce simmer uncovered over medium-low heat. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider De Laurentiis says you should let the sauce simmer until it thickens, which will take around 15 minutes. While my sauce simmered, I started cooking the pasta. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I brought a large pot of salted water to a boil over high heat, then threw in the bucatini. De Laurentiis says the noodles should be cooked until they're tender but still firm to the bite, which takes about eight to 10 minutes depending on your stove. After my sauce had finished simmering, I added the cheese. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I stirred in the Parmesan cheese and added another pinch of salt and black pepper. Then I took my sauce off the heat. Once my pasta was ready, I drained the noodles and added them to the sauce. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I gave everything a good mix so my noodles were fully coated. Then I transferred the pasta to a serving bowl and added the meatballs, as well as my remaining parsley and pecorino Romano cheese. Dinner was served! And De Laurentiis' stuffed meatballs easily stole the show. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider It's been a very long time since my parents were impressed with a meatball recipe , but they were huge fans of De Laurentiis' version. The meatballs were juicy, moist, and tender — the perfect texture — and packed with tons of flavor. Both cheeses worked really well as a stuffing, and everyone in the family had a different favorite. I'd love to make these again with smoked mozzarella, but you could try this with so many different cheeses. I thought De Laurentiis' bucatini noodles were well-made and had a lovely taste, but I wish the sauce had more oomph. I had thrown in two extra ounces of pancetta, which we realized made the sauce just a tad too salty. Next time, I'd also make the sauce thicker and add some red wine or cream to give it more flavor. Bucatini is the perfect vehicle to carry a thick red sauce, and I just wanted more from the All'Amatriciana. But De Laurentiis' meatballs truly blew my family away. I know we're going to be making them over and over again. Read the original article on Business Insider

I placed a cube of cheese in the center of every meatball.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

I used my finger to make an indentation in each meatball, where I tucked in a piece of cheese. I then reshaped the ball so the cheese was completely covered and firmly in the center. 

Since I was using two different cheeses, I made half of the meatballs with smoked Gouda and the other half with mozzarella. 

I placed my meatballs on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper and threw them into the oven.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

De Laurentiis says the meatballs should bake for 15 minutes until fully cooked through, but it took an extra seven minutes for my meatballs to finish.

Every oven is different, so just keep an eye on them!

While my meatballs were baking, I got started on the pasta sauce.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

Amatriciana is traditionally made with guanciale, but De Laurentiis said she uses pancetta instead "because it's much easier to find in grocery stores!"

After drizzling some olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat, I added the pancetta and let it cook for six minutes, stirring constantly.

You'll know it's ready when the pancetta turns golden brown.

I used a slotted spoon to remove the pancetta, then added the onions.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

I let the onions cook for five minutes.

Next, I added the garlic and red pepper flakes.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

I let everything cook together for about 30 seconds, until the garlic became fragrant.

I added the crushed tomatoes and threw the pancetta back into the pan.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

I seasoned everything with half a teaspoon of salt and half a teaspoon of freshly ground black pepper.

Then I let my sauce simmer uncovered over medium-low heat.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

De Laurentiis says you should let the sauce simmer until it thickens, which will take around 15 minutes.

While my sauce simmered, I started cooking the pasta.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

I brought a large pot of salted water to a boil over high heat, then threw in the bucatini.

De Laurentiis says the noodles should be cooked until they're tender but still firm to the bite, which takes about eight to 10 minutes depending on your stove. 

After my sauce had finished simmering, I added the cheese.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

I stirred in the Parmesan cheese and added another pinch of salt and black pepper. Then I took my sauce off the heat. 

Once my pasta was ready, I drained the noodles and added them to the sauce.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

I gave everything a good mix so my noodles were fully coated. Then I transferred the pasta to a serving bowl and added the meatballs, as well as my remaining parsley and pecorino Romano cheese. 

Dinner was served! And De Laurentiis' stuffed meatballs easily stole the show.

Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider

It's been a very long time since my parents were impressed with a meatball recipe, but they were huge fans of De Laurentiis' version.  

The meatballs were juicy, moist, and tender — the perfect texture — and packed with tons of flavor. Both cheeses worked really well as a stuffing, and everyone in the family had a different favorite. I'd love to make these again with smoked mozzarella, but you could try this with so many different cheeses. 

I thought De Laurentiis' bucatini noodles were well-made and had a lovely taste, but I wish the sauce had more oomph. I had thrown in two extra ounces of pancetta, which we realized made the sauce just a tad too salty. Next time, I'd also make the sauce thicker and add some red wine or cream to give it more flavor. Bucatini is the perfect vehicle to carry a thick red sauce, and I just wanted more from the All'Amatriciana. 

But De Laurentiis' meatballs truly blew my family away. I know we're going to be making them over and over again.

items.title: AI's new North Star: Intelligence per dollar
items.summary: Star trails centered around the North Star. Science Photo Library/Reuters Connect A version of this story originally appeared in the BI Tech Memo newsletter. Sign up for the weekly BI Tech Memo newsletter here . The AI industry has spent the past few years obsessing over one question: Who has the smartest model ? That still matters. But a new north star is emerging: how much useful intelligence can be delivered for each dollar spent. A lot of models are now good enough for many business tasks. Once that happens, buyers start caring less about the absolute best model and more about the cost of getting reliable work done with AI. Eugene Kim 's recent scoop on Amazon's rebuild of Alexa+ is a good example. Internal documents show the company routing more requests to its own less-powerful AI, while avoiding unnecessary calls to Anthropic's pricier, higher-performing models. The goal was not to make Alexa use the smartest model every time. It was to use expensive intelligence only when the job required it. "This is a very strong and real trend," said Kylan Gibbs , CEO of Inworld , which develops powerful voice AI. "We're reaching a state where many models are good enough, and in that context, it really becomes about efficiency." His company has created separate research teams focused on making Inworld models cheaper and faster to run, not just more intelligent. So, what's the best AI model, per dollar of intelligence? This is harder to answer than when the industry was focused on pure performance. Still, Peter Gostev , AI capability lead at Arena AI , shared four things to consider: How good is it? How reliably does the model complete real work? What does it charge? Compare the cost of both reading a request and producing an answer. Some model providers charge more for especially large jobs. How much can it reuse? Reusing information already processed can dramatically reduce the bill. How much work does it take? A model that's cheap on a per-token basis may still cost more if it needs extra steps or repeated attempts to finish the job. Peter was reluctant to share a clear ranking of AI models based on these criteria, partly because this trend is so new. However, this is becoming increasingly clear: The smartest model may still win the headlines, but the model that delivers the most useful work for the money will win the market. items.title: Meta Working on Crushingly Sad AI App That Tells Bedtime Stories to Children, for “Tired” Parents
items.summary: Meta is testing an app that uses AI to automate bedtime stories for children. The future is here, folks — and boy, is it depressing. The app, first caught by 9to5Mac , is called “StoryKit.” (It’s not yet available in the US; Meta confirmed to TechCrunch that it’s currently testing StoryKit in pilot countries.) Per a webpage for the app, parents pick a character either by creating one or taking a “photo of their favorite toy or person to bring them to life,” then describe a setting or world for the story to take place in. They can also ask the story to include a specific lesson or moral, which the app says will allow it to “weave in values like kindness, courage, or empathy without it feeling like a lecture.” The resulting story can be read aloud by a human — or, of course, an AI voice can narrate instead. According to Meta, this is a lifeline for exhausted parents. “Tired after a long day but want to give your kids a special bedtime story?” reads the app’s webpage. “StoryKit uses Al to help you create personalized bedtime stories in seconds. No more guilt about screen time. Just beautiful, unique stories made with love.” Let’s be real: this app is amazingly sad. There are a lot of busy and exhausted parents, but outsourcing the emotional and creative labor of bedtime stories to machines is a wildly bleak proposition. Meta claims that this app will help parents feel less guilty about their kids’ screen time, but is having an AI voice read an AI-generated bedtime story to your kids that much different from plopping them in front of an iPad? There are also countless human-written children’s books out there to choose from, if parents don’t enjoy coming up with stories with their kids on the spot. If you’re feeling guilty about screens, perhaps the answer is paper-bound books, not robots. All in all: kids’ bedtime stories — bonding moments between parents and their children, in which parents can foster creativity and impart what they believe to be important lessons — aren’t exactly spaces begging for tech disruption. In fact, this is an area where we probably need less tech, not more. More on kids and AI: The Proliferation of Deepfakes Is Profoundly Changing the Way Teenagers Use the Internet The post Meta Working on Crushingly Sad AI App That Tells Bedtime Stories to Children, for “Tired” Parents appeared first on Futurism .

items.title: How routing keys isolate Kafka consumer tests on a shared broker
items.summary: A change to a service that consumes from Kafka is not validated until it has run against the real system: real partitions, real consumer groups, the events other teams produce. Coding agents sharpen the requirement. An agent iterating on a consumer needs to publish an event, observe what its change did downstream, read the failure and rerun, many times per change and in parallel with every other agent’s loops. That only works if a realistic environment is available on demand, for every change. “Testing Kafka consumers is hard. You have to deploy Kafka, producers, consumers, and other service dependencies to validate flows e2e. There is a better pattern.” For synchronous services, the architectural pattern we enable at Signadot delivers exactly that: lightweight ephemeral environments on a shared cluster. Instead of duplicating the stack per change, you run one shared environment continuously deployed from main and deploy only the changed service next to it. Test requests carry a tag, each hop routes tagged traffic to the version under test, and everything else falls through to the shared stable versions. That model rides on request routing, and request routing stops at the first Kafka topic. Nothing between a producer and its consumers picks a destination per message, so the tag that isolates a change everywhere else in the system stops meaning anything at the async hop. Extending the model across that hop takes three mechanisms: a routing key that rides the message, producers that stamp it, and consumers that filter on it. The rest is detail, and the detail is where the pattern succeeds or fails. Why request routing stops at the topic A synchronous call passes through something that can choose a destination per request: a sidecar, a proxy, a client library. A Kafka record is written once and then pulled by every subscribed consumer group at its own pace and its own offset. There is no delivery-time decision point to hook. “The tag that isolates a change everywhere else in the system stops meaning anything at the async hop.” Deploying a changed consumer next to the stable one fails both ways available to you. Put it in the stable consumer group and partition assignment splits the topic between the two versions arbitrarily. Give it a separate group and both versions process every message, doubling every side effect. The contamination runs in both directions. The version under test executes unreviewed code against other people’s messages and writes the results into a shared downstream state. The stable consumer processes your test events, so you cannot tell whether the new code handled them. And because an async flow leaves no request chain to follow, the contamination is hard to even see. The standard workarounds trade the wrong things. A duplicated cluster per environment means brokers, connectors, schema registry, and seed data drifting from production from day one. Per-environment topics push the cost into topic lifecycle automation and per-environment rewiring of every producer and consumer config. A single-node throwaway broker from Testcontainers is the right tool for unit-level consumer logic and says nothing about the shared system. The fix is a routing key that rides the message Give each test deployment an opaque routing key, k7 in the examples below. Tag the initiating test request with that key at the edge. On the synchronous legs, the key travels in OpenTelemetry baggage, and you need only the context propagation part of OpenTelemetry, not tracing. At publish time, copy the key from the request context into the record headers. Headers, not payload: the message body stays untouched, and consumers can filter without deserializing. Every mainstream broker has an equivalent slot: message attributes in SQS and Pub/Sub, headers in AMQP. Put the copying in shared code, not in each service. OpenTelemetry producer instrumentation can do it, or a thin internal wrapper around the standard client, so a service publishes exactly as before and propagation stays uniform across teams. The key names the test, not the workload This is the detail that makes the pattern compose. The key identifies the test context that caused a message, not the deployment that produced it. A stable producer serving a request tagged k7 emits records tagged k7. “The key identifies the test context that caused a message, not the deployment that produced it.” That is how a consumer change gets tested in isolation. No test version of the producer exists; the stable producer stamps your key, and only your consumer version picks it up. On the consumer side, restore the key from the headers into the processing context before the handler runs, so every downstream call and every further publish carries it onward. Isolation holds only while that chain is unbroken. Flows without an originating request need the key seeded explicitly, and change data capture (CDC) is the sharpest case: the connector has no request context, so the key goes into a metadata column and the connector copies it into headers. Consumers filter, and exactly one version processes each message Every consumer version subscribes to the shared topic and receives everything. The decision is per message, in a should-process gate ahead of the handler. A test consumer processes a message only when the header key matches its own test context. The stable consumer processes untagged traffic, plus tagged messages whose key no live test consumer claims. The fallback clause does two jobs. A producer-only test still works, because stable consumers handle its tagged messages downstream. And another test’s key never reaches your version under test. The net effect: exactly one consumer version processes each message. Consumer groups keep the versions from interfering at the offset level. Each test consumer joins a fresh group named after its deployment, tracks its own offsets, and starts at the latest offset so it does not replay the topic’s backlog. The stable group’s commits are untouched. The group is created with the test deployment and deleted with it. Consumers learn which keys are claimed from a small in-cluster mapping service that holds key-to-deployment state. Poll it and cache the result, or stream updates from it. The gate consults the cached map on every message. A validation run, end-to-end Here is the loop as an agent runs it. The agent changes the payment consumer and deploys the modified version alongside the stable one, with key k7, its own consumer group, and a registration in the routing map. The agent then sends a request tagged k7 at the edge, or produces a tagged event directly. The stable order producer stamps k7 into the records it publishes. On the topic, those records sit interleaved with everyone else’s traffic. The k7 consumer processes them, the stable consumer skips them, and the effects flow downstream still carrying k7. The agent asserts on downstream state, reads whatever failed, patches the consumer, redeploys and reruns. Between iterations, only the changed deployment moves. When the change merges, deleting the test deployment removes the group and the map entry, and nothing else in the system changes. Dozens of these loops run on one cluster at once, each seeing real partitions, real rebalancing, and real traffic from producers other teams operate. A few things to keep in mind The routing key is not the partition key. Each version sees its messages in partition order, but a test that depends on strict ordering across interleaved tests and production traffic will not get it. Batch consumers must split each batch by key before processing. The routing map cache is stale for a few seconds around deployment create and delete, which is exactly when a first message tends to arrive. Some cases still call for duplicated infrastructure: when the broker configuration is itself the thing under test, and when compliance requires hard tenant separation. Everything else gets a different cost model, a test environment that amounts to the changed services plus a consumer group. There is also a second approach worth knowing. Instead of routing on a shared topic, you can spin up ephemeral topics and point the producers and consumers at them for the life of the test. That swaps the routing work for reconfiguration: every producer and consumer in the flow has to be rewired to the new topic names when the environment comes up, and switched back when it goes away. Our resource plugin framework is built for exactly this. A plugin provisions the topics on sandbox creation, tears them down on deletion, and passes the connection details into the sandboxed workloads. A concrete check for your own system: trace how the last schema change to a shared topic was validated before merge, and how long it waited for an environment where that was possible. If the answer involves a calendar, that topic is where your isolation ends and where your agents will queue. We built Signadot around this pattern , and it plugs into the Kafka implementation you already have. items.title: My dad came to live with me after getting sick, and my sister moved in to help. His long-term care costs us over $4,000 a month.
items.summary: Teri Carlyle is caring for her father, who lives with her and her sister. Teri Carlyle Teri Carlyle shares her family's journey of caregiving for her aging father in Vallejo, California. Carlyle manages her father's long-term care costs, as he lives with her and her sister. Carlyle said she's trying to cut expenses, but will never put her father in a facility. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Teri Carlyle, 58, who lives with her sister and father in Vallejo, California. Carlyle said the multigenerational living arrangement has worked well for them and allowed the family to cut costs. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. I've had an amazing life. I knew my great-grandparents, so I know what it looks like to age with dignity and grace. My grandparents were loving and supported us. I've traveled the world, and I'm a director of finance and operations at a nonprofit. My parents were married for 64 years when my mom died. My mom retired from the federal government , while my dad retired from Sears. They owned a motorhome and traveled the country for seven months out of the year. They had joined all these RV clubs. But when my parents got sick, they came to live with me. Are you paying for your own or your loved one's long-term care? Do you have thoughts to share about long-term care in the US? To share your story with a reporter, please fill out this quick form . My parents' health started to decline In 2021, my father had a stroke. Although he wasn't paralyzed, he started having mobility issues, which put him in a wheelchair. My mom was my dad's primary caregiver . But one day in April 2023, I was at home working when my mom passed out. Little did we know that she had a heart problem . She was healthy for most of her life, and this was completely out of the blue. Her legs started swelling. Both of them needed more formal care, which we knew we had to pay for out of pocket. I rented out my parents' house in 2022, and they both moved in with me. It wasn't until two weeks before she died that we found out how severe her condition was. She was in the ER in January 2024. She was dying, and the doctor didn't know if she had weeks, months, or years left. Luckily, she had the foresight to set up her retirement so that, when she died, my dad would still get a retirement check from her. She was earning around $4,600 monthly, but after she died, it dropped to $2,800. We had to find a way to make up this difference. In May 2025, my father woke up one morning and wasn't able to use any words We went to the hospital with him. He was asleep for three weeks, and we didn't know what was going on. My sister and I didn't leave his side the entire time. Eventually, he started coming back to himself. I now have a caregiver who comes to my house to bathe and feed him, and we have another person come in the evening to do the same. Teri Carlyle said she's encouraged her father to be as active as possible. Teri Carlyle It's a blessing that my parents' house is paid for. My sister's house, which is right across the street, has a very small mortgage . Once my mom passed, we were all overwhelmed, and I told my sister that I couldn't care for Dad by myself, so my sister moved in with me, too. My dad is able to be here with us, and there's always someone around. We know we will never put him in a facility. We hired a caregiver to come in during the day We're able to function pretty well. We pay $480 for a monthly personal trainer to work with my father and more than $3,000 a month for caregiving services . There are also insurance costs. We also take him to sporting events, concerts, and movies every now and then. My dad gets Social Security and receives my mom's government pension. I help make up the difference. My brother and his wife usually buy groceries and other things to help out. My sister takes care of some tasks, like hiring a barber who comes to the house. We're trying to find ways to cut costs We want to sell my parents' motorhome, but it's up to my dad to decide whether he doesn't want it anymore. We know we have to let some other things go, such as his car. I'm also trying to think of other ways to increase our revenue, such as renting out one of our houses — either mine or my sister's. Our bank accounts look different from when our mom was alive, but we also don't want to take on too many responsibilities, like side hustles, that would take away from being with our dad. I realized that we take our elders for granted We don't spend enough time with our elders to gain all that we can from them. Everyone needs to have hard and uncomfortable conversations while everyone is healthy, and see what everyone wants for their lives. Younger people should live their best lives because, one day, they might have to come home and take care of their parents, and there shouldn't be resentment that they didn't get to do anything when they had the ability to. People think of caregiving as a burden . I'm living through a beautiful nightmare because it's truly an act of love to be able to take care of my parents and let them see that I love them. items.summary_html:
Teri Carlyle is caring for her father, who lives with her and her sister.

Teri Carlyle

  • Teri Carlyle shares her family's journey of caregiving for her aging father in Vallejo, California.
  • Carlyle manages her father's long-term care costs, as he lives with her and her sister.
  • Carlyle said she's trying to cut expenses, but will never put her father in a facility.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Teri Carlyle, 58, who lives with her sister and father in Vallejo, California. Carlyle said the multigenerational living arrangement has worked well for them and allowed the family to cut costs. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

I've had an amazing life. I knew my great-grandparents, so I know what it looks like to age with dignity and grace. My grandparents were loving and supported us. I've traveled the world, and I'm a director of finance and operations at a nonprofit.

My parents were married for 64 years when my mom died. My mom retired from the federal government, while my dad retired from Sears. They owned a motorhome and traveled the country for seven months out of the year. They had joined all these RV clubs.

But when my parents got sick, they came to live with me.

Are you paying for your own or your loved one's long-term care? Do you have thoughts to share about long-term care in the US? To share your story with a reporter, please fill out this quick form.

My parents' health started to decline

In 2021, my father had a stroke. Although he wasn't paralyzed, he started having mobility issues, which put him in a wheelchair. My mom was my dad's primary caregiver.

But one day in April 2023, I was at home working when my mom passed out. Little did we know that she had a heart problem. She was healthy for most of her life, and this was completely out of the blue. Her legs started swelling.

Both of them needed more formal care, which we knew we had to pay for out of pocket. I rented out my parents' house in 2022, and they both moved in with me.

It wasn't until two weeks before she died that we found out how severe her condition was. She was in the ER in January 2024. She was dying, and the doctor didn't know if she had weeks, months, or years left.

Luckily, she had the foresight to set up her retirement so that, when she died, my dad would still get a retirement check from her. She was earning around $4,600 monthly, but after she died, it dropped to $2,800. We had to find a way to make up this difference.

In May 2025, my father woke up one morning and wasn't able to use any words

We went to the hospital with him. He was asleep for three weeks, and we didn't know what was going on. My sister and I didn't leave his side the entire time. Eventually, he started coming back to himself.

I now have a caregiver who comes to my house to bathe and feed him, and we have another person come in the evening to do the same.

Teri Carlyle said she's encouraged her father to be as active as possible.

Teri Carlyle

It's a blessing that my parents' house is paid for. My sister's house, which is right across the street, has a very small mortgage. Once my mom passed, we were all overwhelmed, and I told my sister that I couldn't care for Dad by myself, so my sister moved in with me, too.

My dad is able to be here with us, and there's always someone around. We know we will never put him in a facility.

We hired a caregiver to come in during the day

We're able to function pretty well. We pay $480 for a monthly personal trainer to work with my father and more than $3,000 a month for caregiving services. There are also insurance costs.

We also take him to sporting events, concerts, and movies every now and then.

My dad gets Social Security and receives my mom's government pension. I help make up the difference. My brother and his wife usually buy groceries and other things to help out. My sister takes care of some tasks, like hiring a barber who comes to the house.

We're trying to find ways to cut costs

We want to sell my parents' motorhome, but it's up to my dad to decide whether he doesn't want it anymore. We know we have to let some other things go, such as his car.

I'm also trying to think of other ways to increase our revenue, such as renting out one of our houses — either mine or my sister's.

Our bank accounts look different from when our mom was alive, but we also don't want to take on too many responsibilities, like side hustles, that would take away from being with our dad.

I realized that we take our elders for granted

We don't spend enough time with our elders to gain all that we can from them. Everyone needs to have hard and uncomfortable conversations while everyone is healthy, and see what everyone wants for their lives.

Younger people should live their best lives because, one day, they might have to come home and take care of their parents, and there shouldn't be resentment that they didn't get to do anything when they had the ability to.

People think of caregiving as a burden. I'm living through a beautiful nightmare because it's truly an act of love to be able to take care of my parents and let them see that I love them.
