items.title: My family of 5 spent $8,600 on a trip to Disney World and Universal. Here's exactly where the money went and how we saved.
items.summary: The author (right) took her family of five to Orlando for a family trip. Courtesy of Lisa Galek My family of 5 spent $8,600 on a trip to Universal Studios and Disney World. The bulk of our money went to flights, two hotel rooms, and park tickets. We saved money by using credit card points. When I started planning a family vacation to Orlando , I knew we wanted to have the full theme park experience — staying at a Universal hotel, visiting the new Epic Universe, adding a Disney day, and enjoying the food and attractions along the way. The result was a six-day vacation that cost $8,620 — and required some careful planning to make the most of our money. Our family includes my husband and me, along with our three kids, ages 18, 15, and 12. At these ages, our children are old enough to appreciate the trip, enjoy all the rides, and make their own memories. The final price tag for our six-day vacation may sound like a lot— and it was. But we also saved money in a few important ways. Here's exactly where our money went. Flying instead of driving saved us two vacation days The first major decision was how to get from Cleveland to Orlando. We spent $1,451 on Frontier Airlines flights for our family of five. We could have driven, but the trip would have taken about 15.5 hours each way. That would have meant losing two full days of vacation time just to sit in the car. For us, flying was worth the extra cost because we wanted to make the most of our time in the parks. We spent $84 to park at Cleveland Hopkins Airport for six days. We also decided not to rent a car in Orlando and instead used Uber to get around when necessary. We spent nearly $5,000 on Universal hotels and park tickets Our biggest expense was $4,948 for our Universal hotel stay and four-day park-to-park tickets. We stayed at Universal's Terra Luna Resort, one of the newest on-site hotels. Terra Luna is considered a Prime Value hotel, and it shares a space-themed design with its sister property, Stella Nova. The hotel's biggest advantage is its location. Since we wanted to spend a lot of time at Epic Universe , staying close to that park was important. Terra Luna guests receive early park admission, which allows us to enter Epic Universe one hour before regular guests each day. The complimentary shuttle ride got us to Epic in less than five minutes, and buses arrived frequently. Booking two rooms was worth the extra cost One challenge with Terra Luna is that the hotel offers only standard rooms that accommodate up to four people, so our party of five needed to book two rooms. At first, paying for two rooms seemed like a big expense, but it turned out to be one of the best decisions we made. We had extra space, privacy, and connecting rooms so we could still easily spend time together. We skipped Express Pass and still rode everything at Epic Universe Our four-day park-to-park tickets included Epic Universe, Universal Studios Florida, and Islands of Adventure. Before the trip, we considered buying Express Passes to skip the lines at Epic, but we were able to experience everything without spending the extra money. Having four days gave us the flexibility to wait for the best times to ride each attraction. We ended up riding every ride at Epic Universe, and the longest wait we had was 45 minutes. That was during July, one of the busiest vacation periods of the year. Our Disney day cost nearly $1,200 We added one day at Disney's Hollywood Studios for $926 in tickets. The author's family spent most of their family trip at Universal Studios in Orlando, but took one day in Disney World. Courtesy of Lisa Galek Because we only had one day at Disney, we purchased Lightning Lane passes for $250. The passes allowed us to reserve a time for Rise of the Resistance and schedule times for up to three other attractions throughout the day. The strategy worked well. We rode almost everything we wanted except Slinky Dog Dash, which was delayed during our reserved time and never reopened that day. We spent $767 on food, but still found ways to save Food is one area where we decided not to cut back. Part of the fun of going to Universal and Disney parks is trying the themed meals and snacks. We spent $767 on food and drinks, eating at restaurants including Cowfish, Toadstool Cafe, The Three Broomsticks, Sci-Fi Dine-In Theater, Krusty Burger, Lard Lad, Café L'air De La Sirène, and Le Gobelet Noir. One trick we used was ordering kids' meals when they made sense. We kept souvenir spending low When it came to souvenirs, we spent only $37 on three chocolate frogs for our kids. Our children saved up their own money to purchase the souvenirs they wanted, including shirts, treats, and stuffed animals. Credit card rewards and dining credits saved us nearly $2,500 Although the total trip cost was $8,620, we received $1,920 back in travel reimbursements through credit card points. Our final out-of-pocket trip cost was around $6,700. A special booking promotion also helped lower our meal costs. Each of our two hotel rooms included a $300 Universal hotel dining credit, giving us $600 to spend on meals at Terra Luna. The dining credit was extremely convenient and kept our overall food costs down. We used it for daily breakfast, as well as other meals, snacks, and adult beverages at the hotel. The trip was expensive — but worth it for our family An $8,620 vacation is a big expense, but the memories we made were worth every penny. By saving where we could, using rewards strategically, and prioritizing the experiences that mattered most, we were able to enjoy the Orlando trip we wanted without overspending — and create memories our family will cherish for years. items.summary_html:
The author (right) took her family of five to Orlando for a family trip.

Courtesy of Lisa Galek

  • My family of 5 spent $8,600 on a trip to Universal Studios and Disney World.
  • The bulk of our money went to flights, two hotel rooms, and park tickets.
  • We saved money by using credit card points.

When I started planning a family vacation to Orlando, I knew we wanted to have the full theme park experience — staying at a Universal hotel, visiting the new Epic Universe, adding a Disney day, and enjoying the food and attractions along the way.

The result was a six-day vacation that cost $8,620 — and required some careful planning to make the most of our money.

Our family includes my husband and me, along with our three kids, ages 18, 15, and 12. At these ages, our children are old enough to appreciate the trip, enjoy all the rides, and make their own memories.

The final price tag for our six-day vacation may sound like a lot— and it was. But we also saved money in a few important ways.

Here's exactly where our money went.

Flying instead of driving saved us two vacation days

The first major decision was how to get from Cleveland to Orlando.

We spent $1,451 on Frontier Airlines flights for our family of five. We could have driven, but the trip would have taken about 15.5 hours each way. That would have meant losing two full days of vacation time just to sit in the car.

For us, flying was worth the extra cost because we wanted to make the most of our time in the parks.

We spent $84 to park at Cleveland Hopkins Airport for six days. We also decided not to rent a car in Orlando and instead used Uber to get around when necessary.

We spent nearly $5,000 on Universal hotels and park tickets

Our biggest expense was $4,948 for our Universal hotel stay and four-day park-to-park tickets.

We stayed at Universal's Terra Luna Resort, one of the newest on-site hotels. Terra Luna is considered a Prime Value hotel, and it shares a space-themed design with its sister property, Stella Nova.

The hotel's biggest advantage is its location. Since we wanted to spend a lot of time at Epic Universe, staying close to that park was important.

Terra Luna guests receive early park admission, which allows us to enter Epic Universe one hour before regular guests each day. The complimentary shuttle ride got us to Epic in less than five minutes, and buses arrived frequently.

Booking two rooms was worth the extra cost

One challenge with Terra Luna is that the hotel offers only standard rooms that accommodate up to four people, so our party of five needed to book two rooms.

At first, paying for two rooms seemed like a big expense, but it turned out to be one of the best decisions we made. We had extra space, privacy, and connecting rooms so we could still easily spend time together.

We skipped Express Pass and still rode everything at Epic Universe

Our four-day park-to-park tickets included Epic Universe, Universal Studios Florida, and Islands of Adventure.

Before the trip, we considered buying Express Passes to skip the lines at Epic, but we were able to experience everything without spending the extra money.

Having four days gave us the flexibility to wait for the best times to ride each attraction. We ended up riding every ride at Epic Universe, and the longest wait we had was 45 minutes. That was during July, one of the busiest vacation periods of the year.

Our Disney day cost nearly $1,200

We added one day at Disney's Hollywood Studios for $926 in tickets.

The author's family spent most of their family trip at Universal Studios in Orlando, but took one day in Disney World.

Courtesy of Lisa Galek

Because we only had one day at Disney, we purchased Lightning Lane passes for $250. The passes allowed us to reserve a time for Rise of the Resistance and schedule times for up to three other attractions throughout the day.

The strategy worked well. We rode almost everything we wanted except Slinky Dog Dash, which was delayed during our reserved time and never reopened that day.

We spent $767 on food, but still found ways to save

Food is one area where we decided not to cut back. Part of the fun of going to Universal and Disney parks is trying the themed meals and snacks.

We spent $767 on food and drinks, eating at restaurants including Cowfish, Toadstool Cafe, The Three Broomsticks, Sci-Fi Dine-In Theater, Krusty Burger, Lard Lad, Café L'air De La Sirène, and Le Gobelet Noir.

One trick we used was ordering kids' meals when they made sense.

We kept souvenir spending low

When it came to souvenirs, we spent only $37 on three chocolate frogs for our kids.

Our children saved up their own money to purchase the souvenirs they wanted, including shirts, treats, and stuffed animals.

Credit card rewards and dining credits saved us nearly $2,500

Although the total trip cost was $8,620, we received $1,920 back in travel reimbursements through credit card points. Our final out-of-pocket trip cost was around $6,700.

A special booking promotion also helped lower our meal costs. Each of our two hotel rooms included a $300 Universal hotel dining credit, giving us $600 to spend on meals at Terra Luna.

The dining credit was extremely convenient and kept our overall food costs down. We used it for daily breakfast, as well as other meals, snacks, and adult beverages at the hotel.

The trip was expensive — but worth it for our family

An $8,620 vacation is a big expense, but the memories we made were worth every penny.

By saving where we could, using rewards strategically, and prioritizing the experiences that mattered most, we were able to enjoy the Orlando trip we wanted without overspending — and create memories our family will cherish for years.

items.summary: The author writes about the emotion she feels when she picks her son up from summer camp. Courtesy of Lindsay Karp My friend told me something when I was pregnant for the first time that I never forgot. He said, "Having children is like having your heart walking around outside your body." Those words have never felt more true than when my teen is at sleepaway camp. When I became pregnant for the first time over 15 years ago, a friend offered me words I never forgot: "Having children is like having your heart walking around outside your body." His words were sweet, but I didn't fully understand them just yet. When my son was born, those words came to life, but as a stay-at-home mother , he wasn't yet venturing beyond my sight, so I knew he was safe and well in real time. We had another baby a few years later, and as both of my boys grew, these words returned to me often. I missed my son in a whole new way when he was at sleepaway camp My now-15-year-old has been going to sleepaway camp for five summers. At drop off, I say goodbye with a hug and hang onto that feeling of having him in my arms until we're together again. My husband and I descend the hill in our car, a piece of myself left behind in the mountains. For four weeks, I move through life wondering what he's doing, whether he's brushing his teeth and eating his veggies, and if he's happy being many miles from home. Everywhere I go, thoughts of him follow, a reminder that I am not whole without him. From his first summer when the dining hall unexpectedly burned to the ground on day three, making national news and igniting a motherly anxiety I'd never known, all the way to this summer when I had no doubt he would love every moment, saying goodbye has become easier with time. I no longer worry if he's happy or if he knows how to pull the fitted sheet over the corners of his bed, because he's more mature now, and camp has become his favorite place on Earth. But while drop-off day has transformed, pick-up day has not. It's still just as magical as ever. Pick-up day is magical Yesterday, my husband and I arrived at the pavilion where my son's trunk was loaded into our car, and as we drove up the hill towards the cabins, the feeling that hits me every summer on pickup day returned. I fought the happy tears welling in my eyes because no teenager wants to introduce his friends to his crying mother. I played it cool for him, but inside I was glowing. After living a month with a piece of my heart many miles away with only pictures to speak of his well-being (we wrote to him, but responses from him were scarce), being reunited is like having that missing piece of myself returned. We parked in a field between the lower and upper camp and began trekking toward his cabin. As always, campers were savoring their last moments together, reminiscing about occasions so impactful that they had been etched into their memories for a lifetime. My eyes wandered back and forth from cabin deck to cabin deck, anxiously searching for that familiar face I'd been missing. Then, there he was, the absent piece of my puzzle. It's been five years — and he's grown so much — but somehow that moment of reunification feels like the first time he ran to me at preschool pickup . There's no running — and I'm far more excited than he is, this time around — but, still, having him with me again returns me to my equilibrium. My big, strong teenager wrapped his arms around me. And in that moment, I realized there's nothing better than hugging your child on pickup day. It makes every toddler tantrum and teenage meltdown worth it. That hug dissolves every mother-son disagreement, and each time he wanted me at a distance because he considered me embarrassing. It reminds both of us that no matter how old he gets, I will always be there to return to. Those words I heard years ago ring true Those words my friend said to me before my son was born were precise. I felt them the day I left him at preschool for the first time and on the day we dropped him off at sleepaway camp for his first summer. But they became crystal clear when I received my first pickup day hug. My heart, that had been walking around outside my body, finally returned to my chest. And yesterday I felt it all over again. My son is beginning high school this year, growing faster than I anticipated. I know every moment of his high school years won't be easy, but I still have a handful of camp pick-up hugs to look forward to. And that makes the ups and downs of motherhood worth it. From his first summer when the dining hall unexpectedly burned to the ground on day three, making national news and igniting a motherly anxiety I'd never known, all the way to this summer when I had no doubt he would love every moment, saying goodbye has become easier with time.

There's no running — and I'm far more excited than he is, this time around — but, still, having him with me again returns me to my equilibrium.

My son is beginning high school this year, growing faster than I anticipated. I know every moment of his high school years won't be easy, but I still have a handful of camp pick-up hugs to look forward to. And that makes the ups and downs of motherhood worth it.

items.title: Ukrainian troops are pinning their hopes on a new top general after losing their star defense minister
items.summary: Mykhailo Drapatyi was appointed Ukraine's new commander in chief on Tuesday. Ukrainian Presidential Press Office via AP Mykhailo Drapatyi, Ukraine's new commander in chief, is one of the war's most popular generals. Troops told Business Insider they hope he'll bring changes that can help them win the war. Tired of Soviet military culture, they're asking for a leader who's pro-tech and listens to them. Anxious after the shock removal of Ukraine's reformist defense minister, the country's front-line troops say that they've found some solace in a new appointment for another key war role — commander in chief. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy appointed 43-year-old Brig. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi as the country's new top general on Tuesday. For many in Ukraine, the appointment is a monumental shift. Drapatyi is replacing Oleksandr Syrskyi, an older general who joined the military when Ukraine was still a Soviet republic. Syrskyi, 60, has overseen many of Ukraine's victories since early 2024 but has been widely accused of resisting change and sticking to a slower, top-down command style that can cost lives in battle. Ukrainian troops across the front lines celebrated Drapatyi's new appointment, telling Business Insider they anticipate the young general to quickly bring much-needed reforms that could turn the tide of the war in their favor. One Ukrainian uncrewed ground vehicle operator told Business Insider that while he feels that Syrskyi has "undoubtedly entered the history of Ukraine as the general who stopped the Russian offensive at the most difficult moment for the state," he has sincere hope "that General Mykhailo Drapatyi will go down in history as the general who won a victory over Russia." Many see Drapatyi, who's had a string of high-profile victories and a reputation for stabilizing warzones under Russian pressure, as the ideal working partner for Mykhailo Fedorov, who was defense minister until recently. Both are seen as drivers of radical change in a military structure that has dysfunctionally struggled to fully leverage innovation and exploit Russia's weaknesses. Drapatyi, pictured on the far right, is replacing Syrskyi, pictured second from the left. Ukrainian Presidential Press Office via AP "He knows how to listen and keeps his word, even when it comes to small promises," said Fizruk, until recently a strike drone company commander with the 82nd Air Assault Brigade. The major, identified only by his call sign for security purposes, said his former drone unit fought under Drapatyi when the latter oversaw operations in Vovchansk, a city in Kharkiv . Russia launched a major offensive there in May 2024, and Drapatyi was sent to stabilize the northeastern front. Fizruk said Drapatyi planned and executed operations "methodically and effectively," but was also personable. He remembered how the brigadier general would wear a green Ukrainian Armed Forces T-shirt to fit in with the team. "I do have his phone number," Fizruk added. Other Ukrainian troops praised Drapatyi for his track record and openness on tech innovation. Social media has allowed Kyiv's forces to tune in closely to public discourse about the war, even while they're deployed, as civilians and soldiers alike share daily news, feedback, commentary, and scandal. A serviceman checks his phone during a break while performing combat tasks in the Kharkiv direction in Ukraine. Viacheslav Madiievskyi/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images The commander of a UGV unit in the 2nd "Khartia" Corps, who goes by the call sign Mathematician, said Drapatyi was "maybe the best choice" to replace Syrskyi. He described the new commander in chief as forward-thinking in the use of ground robots. Andriy, an enlisted soldier who runs community engagement for the 100th Mechanized Brigade's VORON combat drone unit, told Business Insider that he expected Drapatyi to employ a "more rational approach in the use of personnel," while Alex, an officer in Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces , described Drapatyi as a commander who is willing to see different perspectives but with "real combat experience." He said troops respect his "vision and soft skills," predicting a morale boost. The UGV operator who spoke to Business Insider about his hopes for victory over Russia under Drapatyi's command said that "if the new leadership can make the system more flexible, technological, and able to quickly implement effective solutions from the battlefield, this will be the main criterion for success." He said it's "too early to assess this appointment through the prism of expectations. The war has long shown that it is not individual personalities that are decisive, but the ability of the military system to quickly adapt to new challenges." Today, he said, "the key priorities should be to accelerate the introduction of innovations, shorten the path from combat experience to real changes in the troops, scale up unmanned and robotic systems, and provide commanders in the field with greater freedom to make quick decisions." "Ukraine has accumulated unique combat experience," he said. "Our main advantage should be the ability to learn, adapt, and scale successful solutions faster than the enemy." 'The dream team' A key trigger for Drapatyi's appointment was Fedorov's ousting. The latter had been mired in a rivalry with Syrskyi and other generals in Ukraine's top brass, whom Fedorov said balked at his aggressive reforms and campaigns to root out corruption after he was given the post in January. Syrskyi has publicly denied a rift between him and Fedorov. When Fedorov was left out of Zelenskyy's cabinet last week in a government reshuffle, thousands took to the streets of Kyiv and other major cities to protest. Support for Fedorov seized online discourse about the war, and a prevailing demand among demonstrators was that Syrskyi be fired instead. People gathered in Kyiv to denounce the decision to dismiss Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov after six months in the post. AP Photo/Dan Bashakov Almost immediately, Drapatyi's name surged to the top as the pick for Syrskyi's replacement. "There is a consensus in the military that he is the best possible candidate for the role," said Dmytro Koziatynskyi, a former medic in the Da Vinci Wolves who called for civilians to protest last week. One of Drapatyi's best-known feats was videoed just after Russia invaded Crimea in 2014. At the head of an armored column, Drapatyi ordered the driver of his infantry fighting vehicle to hurtle over a barricade in Mariupol and into battle — a sign of decisive aggression at a time when Ukraine's military was still finding its bearings. View this post on Instagram A post shared by UNITED24Media (@united24.media) Later, he famously led a nighttime breakout of 260 troops surrounded by pro-Russian forces in the Donbas. After Moscow's full-scale invasion, Drapatyi became known as a "firefighter" general urgently deployed to stave off intensified Russian campaigns. Apart from his battlefield track record, Koziatynskyi said Drapatyi is also seen among troops as a "new-wave general who listens to his subordinates." "I believe that Drapatyi and Fedorov would be a dream team that can lead us to victory," Koziatynskyi said. Demonstrators plan to continue calling for Fedorov's return . Though there's no clear sign yet that the 35-year-old politician will be restored to his post, political pressure is mounting on Zelenskyy to reinstate Fedorov, who has rejected offers of advisory roles and said he would only return as defense minister. Fedorov spoke to journalists in a press briefing just after his ousting, in which he highlighted some of the challenges he faced as defense minister. AP Photo/Dan Bashakov Mykola Bielieskov, a researcher for Ukraine's National Institute for Strategic Studies and the war crowdfunding organization Come Back Alive, said the main question for Drapatyi now is who he'd be working with — most importantly, the chief of general staff and defense minister. Several troops told Business Insider are still hoping for a Drapatyi-Fedorov team-up. "If Fedorov returns, it will be better, because during his tenure, we saw many effective changes in the military," said Andriy of the 100th Mechanized Brigade. An officer in the 68th Separate Jaeger Brigade, who goes by the call sign Fierce, said that the pair, as the top leaders, would "give strength to the Armed Forces of Ukraine and restore Ukrainians' faith." 'Far more difficult than he imagines' Drapatyi already had experience in strategic command, having served stints as the leader of Ukraine's Ground Forces and then its Joint Forces Command. Valerii Zaluzhnyi , Ukraine's commander in chief during the war's early years before Syrskyi was appointed, praised Drapatyi in a Telegram post on Thursday but warned of the challenges ahead. "The new commander in chief of Ukraine's Armed Forces will have an incredibly difficult job. Far more difficult than he imagines," Zaluzhnyi wrote. Zaluzhnyi was replaced by Syrskyi in February 2024. Ukrainian Presidential Press Office via AP, File Drapatyi will be inheriting a slew of core issues for Ukraine. One of the most pressing problems is Kyiv's struggle to recruit new soldiers, while its outnumbered, deployed forces are exhausted by years of fighting. "No matter popularity, management of the war would be a challenge, given manpower problems, unfinished corps reforms, and a deficit of skilled people at different levels," Bielieskov said. Fierce, the 68th Separate Jaeger Brigade officer, said he considered Drapatyi a "strong general with great authority." "But we'll see how he performs in practice," he said. 'It seems to me there couldn't have been a better choice, but I'll repeat: We'll have to wait and see." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: OpenAI Launches Health in ChatGPT for US Users, Connecting Apple Health and Medical Records
items.summary: OpenAI is launching Health in ChatGPT for US users, enabling connections to Apple Health and supported medical records so ChatGPT can reference health information during conversations. According to OpenAI, connected medical records, Apple Health data, and related conversations are not used for model training or advertising. The feature is now available to logged-in US users aged 18 and older on web and iOS across Free, Go, Plus, and Pro plans, accessible from the ChatGPT sidebar. Health is not currently available in Codex. Users may still ask health questions without connecting any data. What Health in ChatGPT Does And Models Behind Health Conversations With user permission, ChatGPT can access connected information such as medications, lab results, recent visits, sleep, and activity. It can compare new results with prior tests, summarize changes since the last appointment, or relate sleep, activity, and workouts to a routine. OpenAI states this feature aims to reduce repetitive data entry and support, not replace, care from medical professionals. OpenAI reports that over 300 million people use ChatGPT for health-related questions each week, often with relevant information spread across patient portals, records, apps, and wearables. Earlier this year, OpenAI introduced a dedicated health experience to a limited group of users, requiring a separate space in ChatGPT. OpenAI notes that over 70% of health-related conversations occurred outside this space, prompting the ability to reference health information across all conversations. The Health section in the sidebar remains the place to connect and manage information, view trends, browse synced records, and revisit past health conversations. OpenAI states that GPT-5.5 Instant, available on the Free plan, is better at recognizing when urgent care may be needed, requesting relevant context, explaining uncertainty, and simplifying complex information. GPT-5.6 Sol, available to paid users, is described as OpenAI’s most advanced health model, with improved performance on tasks requiring complex reasoning. OpenAI collaborates with hundreds of physicians to develop health scenarios and assessment rubrics for accuracy, safety, communication, context awareness, completeness, and escalation. The company reports that all GPT-5.6 models outperformed GPT-5.5 on HealthBench Professional, its evaluation for challenging health tasks. OpenAI emphasizes that ChatGPT may still make mistakes and does not replace qualified medical professionals, encouraging users to verify important information with a healthcare provider. Privacy and Data Controls: How to Connect Health Information And Access It OpenAI states that Health is built with layered privacy and security safeguards. All ChatGPT conversations are encrypted at rest and in transit, and information connected in Health receives additional encryption. Connected medical records and Apple Health information, and conversations that use them, are excluded from foundation model training and ad targeting regardless of the user's model-training setting. Conversations that do not use this data follow the user's standard model-training settings, adjustable in Settings, then Data Controls. By default, ChatGPT requests permission before using connected records to personalize responses. Users can approve each request or choose to always allow access, which disables prompts, by adjusting Settings under Plugins and Health. Users can disconnect Health information at any time in Health under Accounts. OpenAI states that data from a disconnected source is deleted from its systems within 30 days, though information already in conversation history remains until those conversations are deleted. Memories are not created directly from connected medical records or Apple Health information. Users can use Temporary Chat or disable memory in Settings under Memory. OpenAI states that before ChatGPT takes action in another connected plugin that could disclose Health information, additional safeguards verify that sharing matches the request, and some sensitive actions require confirmation. Users who want responses based on their own data can connect Apple Health, supported medical records from US hospital systems, One Medical, or Function Health. Open Health from the sidebar or More menu in ChatGPT, select "Get started," and follow the guided connection process. Allow the information to sync, which maAllow the information to sync, which may take a few minutes. You can connect additional accounts during or after syncing. Confirm that data sharing to Apple Health is enabled, since ChatGPT can only use what those apps make available through Apple Health. Some proprietary scores may not transfer. Review connected conditions and medications, remove any that are no longer relevant, and add missing details, including family health history. Update outdated entries, as connected information may not always be current, and verify important details against the original source. Once synced, users can ask questions anywhere in ChatGPT and add @Health to a message to explicitly request health context. Health in ChatGPT is now available to US users aged 18 and older on web and iOS across Free, Go, Plus, and Pro plans. OpenAI has not announced availability outside the US, support in Codex, or an Android release timeline. Connected information may not always be complete or current. OpenAI advises users to verify important details with the original source and consult a healthcare provider for medical decisions. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. items.summary_html:
OpenAI is launching Health in ChatGPT for US users, enabling connections to Apple Health and supported medical records so ChatGPT can reference health information during conversations.

According to OpenAI, connected medical records, Apple Health data, and related conversations are not used for model training or advertising.

The feature is now available to logged-in US users aged 18 and older on web and iOS across Free, Go, Plus, and Pro plans, accessible from the ChatGPT sidebar.

Health is not currently available in Codex. Users may still ask health questions without connecting any data.

What Health in ChatGPT Does And Models Behind Health Conversations

With user permission, ChatGPT can access connected information such as medications, lab results, recent visits, sleep, and activity. It can compare new results with prior tests, summarize changes since the last appointment, or relate sleep, activity, and workouts to a routine. OpenAI states this feature aims to reduce repetitive data entry and support, not replace, care from medical professionals.

OpenAI reports that over 300 million people use ChatGPT for health-related questions each week, often with relevant information spread across patient portals, records, apps, and wearables.

Earlier this year, OpenAI introduced a dedicated health experience to a limited group of users, requiring a separate space in ChatGPT.

OpenAI notes that over 70% of health-related conversations occurred outside this space, prompting the ability to reference health information across all conversations.

The Health section in the sidebar remains the place to connect and manage information, view trends, browse synced records, and revisit past health conversations.

OpenAI states that GPT-5.5 Instant, available on the Free plan, is better at recognizing when urgent care may be needed, requesting relevant context, explaining uncertainty, and simplifying complex information.

GPT-5.6 Sol, available to paid users, is described as OpenAI’s most advanced health model, with improved performance on tasks requiring complex reasoning.

OpenAI collaborates with hundreds of physicians to develop health scenarios and assessment rubrics for accuracy, safety, communication, context awareness, completeness, and escalation.

The company reports that all GPT-5.6 models outperformed GPT-5.5 on HealthBench Professional, its evaluation for challenging health tasks.

OpenAI emphasizes that ChatGPT may still make mistakes and does not replace qualified medical professionals, encouraging users to verify important information with a healthcare provider.

Privacy and Data Controls: How to Connect Health Information And Access It

OpenAI states that Health is built with layered privacy and security safeguards. All ChatGPT conversations are encrypted at rest and in transit, and information connected in Health receives additional encryption.

Connected medical records and Apple Health information, and conversations that use them, are excluded from foundation model training and ad targeting regardless of the user's model-training setting.

Conversations that do not use this data follow the user's standard model-training settings, adjustable in Settings, then Data Controls.

By default, ChatGPT requests permission before using connected records to personalize responses. Users can approve each request or choose to always allow access, which disables prompts, by adjusting Settings under Plugins and Health.

Users can disconnect Health information at any time in Health under Accounts. OpenAI states that data from a disconnected source is deleted from its systems within 30 days, though information already in conversation history remains until those conversations are deleted.

Memories are not created directly from connected medical records or Apple Health information. Users can use Temporary Chat or disable memory in Settings under Memory.

OpenAI states that before ChatGPT takes action in another connected plugin that could disclose Health information, additional safeguards verify that sharing matches the request, and some sensitive actions require confirmation.

Users who want responses based on their own data can connect Apple Health, supported medical records from US hospital systems, One Medical, or Function Health.

  1. Open Health from the sidebar or More menu in ChatGPT, select "Get started," and follow the guided connection process.
  2. Allow the information to sync, which maAllow the information to sync, which may take a few minutes. You can connect additional accounts during or after syncing. Confirm that data sharing to Apple Health is enabled, since ChatGPT can only use what those apps make available through Apple Health. Some proprietary scores may not transfer.
  3. Review connected conditions and medications, remove any that are no longer relevant, and add missing details, including family health history.
  4. Update outdated entries, as connected information may not always be current, and verify important details against the original source.

Once synced, users can ask questions anywhere in ChatGPT and add @Health to a message to explicitly request health context.

Health in ChatGPT is now available to US users aged 18 and older on web and iOS across Free, Go, Plus, and Pro plans. OpenAI has not announced availability outside the US, support in Codex, or an Android release timeline.

Connected information may not always be complete or current. OpenAI advises users to verify important details with the original source and consult a healthcare provider for medical decisions.

items.title: I passed up promotions for a 4-day workweek. Spending time with my kids is more important.
items.summary: The author (not pictured) works remotely and has a four-day workweek, which allows him to spend more time with his family. hobo_018/Getty Images I've turned down opportunities in my company for a four-day workweek. On the side, I've built a freelance career. Doing this has allowed me to spend time with my kids. People at my company don't understand, but it's what's right for me. When my wife and I moved from Calgary to Nelson , British Columbia, in 2017, we were mostly thinking about our kids. We wanted them to have space, freedom, and a childhood spent outdoors in nature rather than in a car seat during rush hour. What I didn't think much about, though, was what the move would do to my career. After we moved, I was fortunate enough to keep my corporate job and go fully remote . Over the years that followed, I made a series of choices that, from the outside, probably look like a career stalling out. Instead of working long hours in an office in a downtown high-rise, I work four days a week from our spare bedroom in a small town of 11,000 people. And I've turned down multiple opportunities to step into a lead role within my company. None of that happened by accident. Every part of it was deliberate, and I'd make the same choices again. But I've learned that when you opt out of the ladder on purpose, the people around you struggle to read it as a decision. They read it as a problem. People assume I'm waiting for something better Colleagues, friends, and family members will often ask me how the four-day thing is "working out," in the same tone you'd use to ask about a medical treatment. Nobody has ever said " you're wasting your potential " out loud, but the assumption is right there underneath the conversation: that I'm stuck in a holding pattern, that this is temporary, that eventually I'll get serious about my career. The truth is, I already did get serious. I just got serious about something else. I take Fridays off to homeschool and spend time with my kids. I get to drop off and pick them up from school. I coach their soccer teams. And I've built a second career as a freelance writer that exists entirely in the hours a promotion would have taken. While this picture may not look like career ambition from the outside, it's the most ambitious thing I've ever done. The trade-off is real, and I made it anyway I want to be honest about what this costs, because I don't think choosing time over a job title is free. I make less money than I would in a lead role. Which can be stressful at times, considering I have a mortgage and two kids. I feel that math every month. I've also given up a kind of professional standing. In meetings, I'm not the go-to person the room turns to. Decisions get made in conversations I'm not in. Some of the work I'd be genuinely good at goes to other people, and occasionally that stings more than I expect it to. And I've noticed the cost of being on a non-management track for years. You become slightly harder to place, and people stop thinking of you when something big comes up. The old adage of "out of sight, out of mind" rings true in my life. But here's what I got in exchange: I've been home for nearly every school pickup and sick day my kids have ever had. I was there for the years when my daughter still wanted to tell me about her day, and I'm still here now that she's almost 12 and doesn't always want to. I'm well aware that window of time in my kids' lives is closing. The promotion will still be there. This time with my kids, however, will not. My kids don't know I gave anything up The funny thing is that the people this decision was made for have no idea I made it. My kids don't know that I said no to a promotion . They don't know there was a version of my life with a bigger salary and less of me in it. They just know that I'm always around, that I'm the one at the soccer field on Saturdays, and that when they walk in the door after school, someone is there. To them, that's not a sacrifice. It's just how things are. And I've come to understand that's the whole point. A choice like this only works if it's invisible to the people it's for. If my kids ever had to be grateful for it, it would mean I'd made it about me. I've stopped explaining myself For a long time, I felt a need to justify the four-day workweek. I'd over-explain, list the reasons, and make sure people knew I was still productive, ambitious, and valuable, as though I owed the world an explanation. I don't do that anymore. Part of it is age. I'm 39, and I've spent enough years approaching my work like I'm always job hunting to know that professional security is mostly an illusion anyway. Titles disappear. Budgets shrink. Companies restructure. The people climbing hardest are not necessarily any safer than I am. But mostly, I've just made peace with being illegible to the people I work with. They see a career that plateaued, while I see a life I built on purpose, one deliberate step at a time. They don't have to understand it. It was never for them anyway. items.title: PUBG at Esports World Cup 2026 Reaches Grand Finals With Made in Thailand Topping the Group Stage
items.summary: The PUBG: Battlegrounds tournament at the Esports World Cup 2026 takes place from July 21 to 26 in Paris, France. Twenty-four teams are competing in a two-stage format for a $2,025,000 prize pool, as reported by Dot Esports. Made in Thailand led the Group Stage with 119 points, followed by T1 with 110 and Natus Vincere with 93. The top 16 teams advanced to the Grand Finals, held from July 24 to 26. The event is played in Squads TPP mode on PC. Grand Finals results are pending. Schedule, Format, and Group Stage Results The Group Stage runs from July 21 to 23, followed by the Grand Finals from July 24 to 26. Each stage consists of 18 matches over three days. During the Group Stage, 24 teams were split into three groups of eight and played cross-group round-robin matches, with each team playing 12 matches. The top 16 teams advanced to the Grand Finals; the bottom eight were eliminated. The Grand Finals apply the Smash Rule on Day 3. If a match-point eligible team wins a Chicken Dinner, they secure the championship. Otherwise, the team with the highest total points at the end wins. Made in Thailand led the combined Group Stage standings with 119 points, bolstered by 79 points in Group A vs B matches. T1 placed second with 110 points, and Natus Vincere was third with 93. The top eight Group Stage teams were: Made in Thailand (119), T1 (110), Natus Vincere (93), Twisted Minds (92), Team Falcons (86), Virtus.pro (85), 17 Gaming (76), and GAM Esports (76). The eight teams eliminated after the Group Stage were JD Gaming, SOOPers, R8 Esports, Sharper Esports, Team Nemesis, TYLOO, Petrichor Road, and Four Angry Men. Participating Teams and Prize Pool Distribution The 24 teams were divided into three groups. Group A: Virtus.pro, All Gamers Global (AGAL International), SOOPers, Petrichor Road, TYLOO, Team Vitality, FULL SENSE, and Shadow Esports. Group B: Made in Thailand, Four Angry Men, Twisted Minds, Geekay Esports, Team Nemesis, Team Liquid, GAM Esports, and R8 Esports. Group C: 17 Gaming, Natus Vincere, T1, Gen.G Esports, JD Gaming, Team Falcons, The Vicious, and Sharper Esports. The $2,025,000 prize pool is awarded based on final Grand Finals placement. First place receives $650,000 and 1,000 EWC Club Points; second place receives $300,000 and 750 points; third place receives $200,000 and 500 points. Prize money decreases through the standings, with the 16th-place team receiving $20,000. The eight teams eliminated in the Group Stage receive fixed payouts, from $17,000 for JD Gaming (17th) to $10,000 for Four Angry Men (24th). The MVP Award winner receives an additional $25,000. How to Watch And What to Watch For The PUBG tournament at EWC 2026 is streamed live on PUBG Esports' official Twitch and YouTube channels. Match times follow the Paris event schedule; viewers should convert times to their local timezone to follow the Grand Finals. With the Grand Finals underway, several outcomes remain undecided: whether Made in Thailand can turn its Group Stage lead into a championship, as Grand Finals points reset the standings among the 16 finalists. How the Smash Rule on Day 3 will impact the outcome, since a match-point eligible team can win the tournament with a single Chicken Dinner.The MVP Award race, which offers a separate $25,000 prize. Final placement for the $650,000 top prize, to be confirmed when the Grand Finals conclude on July 26. Dot Esports has not yet published Grand Finals match results or final placements and will provide updates as the finals progress through July 26. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post PUBG at Esports World Cup 2026 Reaches Grand Finals With Made in Thailand Topping the Group Stage appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: New Parody Site Threatens to Replace CEOs With AI for Tiny Fraction of Their Bloated Salaries
items.summary: By now, it should be pretty clear that the corporate executives of the world aren’t exactly into AI because they think it’ll cure cancer. They’re making a different calculation, motivated by simple economics: pretty soon, they believe, AI will be efficient enough to do many or even all workers’ job, removing employee payroll from the corporate equation. That means more money for those at the top, and less time dealing with pesky annoyances like labor rights and health coverage. For that to happen would take a series of technological miracles — as a recent study out of the University of California Berkeley shows, today’s cutting-edge AI tools are still incapable of completing the bulk of real-world tasks at a level comparable to humans. Still, it’s clear executives are hungry for the kind of cost-savings AI could provide. Luckily, a new AI site offers a solution: OverpAId, a distinctly tongue-in-cheek project that facetiously claims to offer an AI-powered replacement for your company’s CEO — or as the site’s landing page puts it , the “world’s first Chief Executive Replacement Engine”. “OverpAId is an Artificial Intelligence built from the ground up to do your CEO’s entire job — strategy, ‘vision,’ motivational all-hands emails — better, faster, and without ever once asking the board for a bigger jet,” the site exclaims. The parodic offering claims to offer helpful features to help your team transition from an expensive human executive to a cheap AI equivalent. These include a “jargon bingo,” an AI-hype press release translator, a “talk to a real executive” chat widget (currently busted), and an ROI calculator that helps users distribute CEO pay packages equally across every remaining employee. It hammers that point repeatedly, pointing out the fact that the average CEO-to-worker pay ratio is an astonishing 290 to 1 at large public companies (which is actually true , incredibly.) While OverpAId is clearly a piece of satire, it gets at something very real: the fact that CEO pay has grown at an astonishing rate , while rank-and-file wages and salaries have crawled at a snails pace, in many cases not even keeping pace with inflation. “Somewhere along the way, the story became: pay the person at the top enough, and the value will trickle down to everyone else,” the site explains. There’s just one problem with that telling: “It hasn’t. It doesn’t. It never really did.” More on AI automation: AI Is Pushing Older Employees Straight Out of the Workforce, New Report Finds The post New Parody Site Threatens to Replace CEOs With AI for Tiny Fraction of Their Bloated Salaries appeared first on Futurism .

items.title: With help from data, art museums are reframing the visitor experience
items.summary: Giovanni Kanter goes to at least one art museum whenever he visits a new city. That’s on top of his regular exploration of galleries in New York, where the 25-year-old ICU nurse lives and studies. He typically discovers new artists and gallery openings through word of mouth, though he has recently started curating his social media feed to serve relevant content (he’s currently in what he terms a “surrealism phase”). He was raised on visual art; he's the son of painter Marianne Gargour and nephew of mixed-media artist Heather Hutchison and painter-printmaker Mark Thomas Kanter . His “exposure-oriented education” featured childhood visits to galleries and shows in and around Dallas, where he grew up, and in France, where he spent time with his grandparents. But Kanter is an exception. Many other young people have a less immersive artistic education, perhaps shaped by occasional school trips or family visits to museums. If they haven’t internalized an instinct for what Kanter calls “moving through the art and absorbing it,” the museum experience is central to how they learn about and understand art. Read full article Comments

items.title: Big Tech accused of stonewalling European social media researchers
items.summary: In the final weeks before Romania’s presidential vote in November 2024, TikTok accounts that had previously spent years posting about manicures or fashion suddenly started promoting a little-known politician named Calin Georgescu. His posts, espousing hard-line views on immigration and anti-Semitic tropes, were viewed 120 million times before the vote. Georgescu, who had previously been polling in the single digits, stunned observers by winning the election’s first round with 23 percent of the vote. In the Netherlands, Adriana Iamnitchi was watching closely. As chair of computational social sciences at Maastricht University, she leads the research into disinformation campaigns. She wanted to know how pro-Georgescu content was being monetized on TikTok through hidden influencer marketing and livestreamed political content. Read full article Comments

items.title: Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and 22 others defended open weights. Anthropic and OpenAI didn’t sign.
items.summary: The fight over open-weight AI entered a new round over the last week. On July 22, White House officials accused China’s Moonshot AI of stealing American IP through distillation and floated sanctions and repercussions. Anthropic’s policy chief called the alleged operation “industrial espionage.” Then the startups showed up, with nearly 200 co-signing a letter to President Trump urging him not to cut off the open models they rely on. On Friday, a statement signed by 25 major organizations warned Washington against “premature restrictions” on open weights. And Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, asked by Axios whether open labs should be allowed to distill closed models, answered that distillation is “fundamental to intelligence.” Let me be clear: Running an open-weight Chinese AI model is not a fringe act, and it’s not disloyal. It’s how many AI-native startups and developers keep their token bills under control because Anthropic and OpenAI are becoming too expensive to build on at scale. Washington wants to draw the line between legitimate openness and Chinese theft. Inside the technology industry, the more revealing line is open versus closed. Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta, and 22 other organizations signed the statement, warning against premature restrictions and defending distillation as a legitimate model-development technique. Anthropic and OpenAI did not sign. For developers, the stakes are not abstract. The affordable model they can download, adapt, and run themselves is exactly what this fight could make harder to access. Developers already picked open weights because of cost Startups are on the front line here. America’s frontier labs priced many of them onto Chinese open weights. Nearly 200 companies, Y Combinator and Proton among them, told the President through the new Little Tech Association not to cut off Chinese open weights, and to use “a scalpel rather than a sledgehammer.” Particle founder Shuail Doshi put it plainly: “There’ll be hundreds of companies that instantly die. It’s great for Anthropic. We’re all going to have to spend money on Anthropic.” Why the panic? It’s the price. I’ve been talking about this for months. Moonshot’s Kimi K3 is a near-frontier model that’s extremely powerful. My colleague Jessica Wachetel ran Kimi K3 head-to-head against Anthropic’s best coding model across a bug fix, a refactor, and a feature build; Kimi K3 wrote the same code as Claude Fable 5 for about a third of the cost . It was roughly four times slower. Claude Fable 5 vs. Kimi K3: same code, a third the cost, four times slower Model Price (in / out) 3-task cost 3-task time Code produced Claude Fable 5 Anthropic $10 / $50 $5.98 ~7 min Baseline Kimi K3 Moonshot · open weight $3 / $15 $2.13 ~28 min Same result Source: The New Stack, Jessica Wachtel’s Fable 5 vs. Kimi K3 head-to-head. Prices are published API rates per 1M tokens (input / output). For a startup counting tokens, four times slower is a fine price for a third of the bill. And they’re paying it. On OpenRouter, Chinese models have accounted for more than 30% of token usage by U.S. customers every week since February, peaking at 46%. OpenRouter is only one slice of the market, but it captures the direction. A meaningful share of developers has already voted with their tokens, routing real workloads toward much-cheaper Chinese models. The pitch for Opus 5, which debuted on Friday , is almost all about cost. It matches or beats Anthropic’s pricier Fable 5 across most of the company’s own benchmarks while costing $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, half of Fable 5 and the same as the older Opus 4.8. Anthropic’s case is cost per finished task, not cost per token: A model that solves the job in one pass can be the cheaper one even at a higher sticker price. It’s a fair point, and it helps narrow the gap. Anthropic cut the price of its frontier performance in half, and yet, it still charges more per token than Kimi K3. The tech industry is split So who actually wants powerful open weights restricted? Anthropic has taken the clearest position, and Axios reports that OpenAI has aligned with it in warning Washington about powerful Chinese open-weight models. The White House, meanwhile, is trying to draw a narrower line by defending open weights generally while punishing Chinese companies it believes used distillation to steal American capabilities. Across from them are many of the companies that supply the chips, clouds, tools, and applications the AI economy runs on. The statement they signed, “ Open Weights and American AI Leadership ,” calls distillation “a widely used technique” and warns policymakers not to conflate legitimate model development with unlawful extraction. Its signatories include Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Mozilla, Palantir, Perplexity, Mistral, and Y Combinator. Anthropic and OpenAI did not sign it. Right now, no ban has been drafted; the White House calls the reporting “baseless speculation,” and our own Amanda Caswell notes that the distillation allegation itself has not been backed by publicly verifiable evidence. But the sides are now on the record. Huang, speaking to Axios , talked about whether open labs should be allowed to distill closed models and rejected the blanket theft framing. American companies should “absolutely” use excellent Chinese models, he said, and distillation itself is “fundamental to intelligence.” He added that privacy and contract violations should still carry consequences. But learning from other systems, in his view, is not theft. It’s how intelligence works. Everyone here is talking about their book. Nvidia sells its chips to Anthropic and OpenAI as eagerly as to anyone running open models, and Microsoft is one of OpenAI’s largest investors. These are not companies with a simple grudge against the closed labs. They have money on both sides, and they still signed this letter anyway. So look at the record. Distilling a model and pirating a book are not the same legal question. But both controversies began with the same accusation: An AI company benefited from material it did not own. The conduct and the law are different, and the hypocrisy is still hard to miss: A court this week approved Anthropic’s 2025 agreement to pay $1.5 billion for downloading and retaining pirated books (the court separately held that using books to train Claude was fair use). Anthropic has also spent more on federal lobbying in the first half of the year than in all of 2025. Its open-source record is real and beside the point: Anthropic backs the open source that expands Claude’s ecosystem, like MCP, while warning Washington about open weights that can compete with it. It’s okay to use open weights This is where it stops being Anthropic’s story and starts being yours. A few weeks ago I wrote about the day a sudden government ruling forced Anthropic to pull Fable , and the developers who had built on it scrambled to swap in other models. They scrambled because Fable is a hosted service, which is the kind of dependency that can change without notice. Open weights are different. If you’ve already downloaded them and can run them on infrastructure you control, they’re far harder to take away than an API someone else owns. The catch is that much of today’s Chinese-model usage still isn’t like that. Many companies and developers access Kimi and other open-weight models through hosted APIs that could disappear overnight if policy changes. Those developers would end up scrambling just like the Fable users did. So don’t just experiment with an open-weight model. Download one. Run it. Know that your stack works before you need it. Not because Kimi is about to disappear, but because the tools you build on can now be switched off by people you’ve never met. The post Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and 22 others defended open weights. Anthropic and OpenAI didn’t sign. appeared first on The New Stack .

The statement they signed, “Open Weights and American AI Leadership,” calls distillation “a widely used technique” and warns policymakers not to conflate legitimate model development with unlawful extraction. A few weeks ago I wrote about the day a sudden government ruling forced Anthropic to pull Fable, and the developers who had built on it scrambled to swap in other models. items.title: A 33-year-old nurse thought her bleeding was caused by hemorrhoids. She was diagnosed with stage 3 colon cancer.
items.summary: Bryce Ramsey, 40, was diagnosed with stage 3 colon cancer in her 30s after dismissing a common symptom for years. Bryce Ramsey Bryce Ramsey, 40, first noticed blood in her stool when she was 26. She dismissed the symptom until it got worse over the years. She was diagnosed with stage 3 colon cancer at 33. When Bryce Ramsey first noticed on-and-off blood in her stool in her 20s, it didn't alarm her too much. She thought the bleeding was due to hemorrhoids caused by either larger bowel movements or childbirth; she had recently given birth to her son, Ashton, who weighed over 10 pounds. She also increasingly felt fatigued, but had an explanation for that, too: she was a registered nurse at the University of Mississippi Medical Center. "I'm tired all the time, but I can justify that, as I work 12-hour shifts," Ramsey, 40, told Business Insider. Ramsey dismissed blood in her stool, one of the most common colon cancer symptoms, for years. Bryce Ramsey By 2019, when the bleeding got worse, she scheduled an appointment with a gastroenterologist. Despite Ramsey only being 33 at the time and having no known family history, her GI found blood in her stool — one of the most common symptoms of colon cancer — too concerning not to schedule her for a colonoscopy. Weeks later, Ramsey was diagnosed with stage 3 colon cancer. "I kind of was in shock but it didn't really sink in," she said. She called Mickee, her then-boyfriend (now-husband), to break the news. "I was just like, 'Okay, well, we've got to get in there and get it out and move on.'" She worked throughout chemo Ramsey working during her chemo treatments. Bryce Ramsey After Ramsey's colonoscopy , she learned she had a polyp that was too large to remove during the procedure. She was scheduled for an appointment with a general surgeon, who diagnosed her with colon cancer. Ramsey learned that the cancer had spread to her lymph nodes. The surgery, performed in November 2019, removed 3 feet of Ramsey's colon and 13 lymph nodes. Before she could start her next phase of treatment, Mickee — who was friends with the surgeon — asked for a favor: could they postpone her treatment by a few weeks so he could trip to New Orleans? After Ramsey's surgery, Mickee popped the question during a Saints football game. "It was really cool," Ramsey said. Bryce Ramsey In January 2020, newly-engaged Ramsey began two types of chemotherapy at once: IV and oral. Ramsey continued to work all throughout chemo. At that point, she was a branch manager for a home health agency. She said she took her computer with her to chemo appointments. The oral chemo led to Ramsey developing severe side effects and losing 17 pounds. "I got really, really, really sick because of that," she said. She also developed cold sensitivity in her fingers. "I had to wear gloves or use a potholder to open my car door," she said, and drinking cold water felt like "blades were in my throat." Ramsey said her son and her recent engagement helped her figure out her "why" for staying strong during treatment. "I was determined no one else was going to raise my little boy but me," she said. A surprise pregnancy months after treatment Ramsey unexpectedly became pregnant with her son, Emree, only a few months after finishing her chemotherapy treatments. Bryce Ramsey Before starting chemotherapy, Ramsey was offered fertility preservation services , as chemotherapy can impair fertility. Because Ramsey and Mickee were in a blended family that included Mickee's children, Ramsey declined. She also didn't use birth control. A few months after finishing chemo in March 2020, Ramsey learned she was pregnant. At first, she was worried about her baby's health: "I'm a complete nervous wreck that I'm going to give birth to a little baby Transformer or something," she said. Ramsey juggled planning her wedding and her pregnancy right after ending her cancer treatment. Bryce Ramsey Still, she felt comforted by a dream she had before her cancer diagnosis . "I'm a very spiritually faith-based person, and I had a dream," she said. "The Lord told me there was going to be another baby, and his name was going to be Luke or Lucas." Ramsey named her son Emree Lucas-Ray Ramsey. She said his name means "'strong ray of light,' which couldn't be any more perfect than from the situation that he came from." Genetic testing helped her family get diagnosed with colon cancer, too Ramsey, who won the 2024 Mrs. Mississippi Plus America pageant, chose colon cancer awareness as her platform. Bryce Ramsey After she was diagnosed with colon cancer, Ramsey learned about genetic testing for mutations that could predispose one to cancer. Ramsey decided to do it, and learned she had Lynch syndrome , a symptomless, inherited condition that increases her risk of developing colon, uterine, and ovarian cancer. Now in remission, Ramsey gets yearly colonoscopies, scans, and bloodwork. She also had a hysterectomy last year, unrelated to cancer, that she said makes her extra relieved because it removes her risk of developing uterine and ovarian cancer as a result of having Lynch syndrome. Since learning she has Lynch syndrome, Ramsey begged her family members to get cancer screenings. "I was the whistleblower," she said. As a result, she said her brother caught his colon cancer at stage 1, her father now has a colostomy bag from his own colon cancer treatment, and her aunt learned that what she thought were gallstones were masses in her colon and liver. Ramsey now advocates for greater awareness around colon cancer and screening for genetic conditions like Lynch syndrome. Bryce Ramsey When Ramsey's sons reach their 20s — the recommended age to start testing for Lynch syndrome — she hopes they'll get tested, too. Ramsey, who was crowned Mrs. Mississippi Plus America in 2024, used the opportunity to spread colon cancer awareness — something she's passionate about. Ramsey has also worked with several advocacy groups and lobbied for funding for genetic testing. "What I say in every one of my speeches is: 'If it doesn't seem right, more than likely it's not,'" Ramsey said. "What's scary is that, as a nurse, I still wasn't fully convinced this might be cancer." Read the original article on Business Insider

Genetic testing helped her family get diagnosed with colon cancer, tooRamsey, who won the 2024 Mrs. Mississippi Plus America pageant, chose colon cancer awareness as her platform.

Bryce Ramsey

After she was diagnosed with colon cancer, Ramsey learned about genetic testing for mutations that could predispose one to cancer. Ramsey decided to do it, and learned she had Lynch syndrome, a symptomless, inherited condition that increases her risk of developing colon, uterine, and ovarian cancer.

Now in remission, Ramsey gets yearly colonoscopies, scans, and bloodwork. She also had a hysterectomy last year, unrelated to cancer, that she said makes her extra relieved because it removes her risk of developing uterine and ovarian cancer as a result of having Lynch syndrome.

Since learning she has Lynch syndrome, Ramsey begged her family members to get cancer screenings. "I was the whistleblower," she said. As a result, she said her brother caught his colon cancer at stage 1, her father now has a colostomy bag from his own colon cancer treatment, and her aunt learned that what she thought were gallstones were masses in her colon and liver.

Ramsey now advocates for greater awareness around colon cancer and screening for genetic conditions like Lynch syndrome.

Bryce Ramsey

When Ramsey's sons reach their 20s — the recommended age to start testing for Lynch syndrome — she hopes they'll get tested, too.

Ramsey, who was crowned Mrs. Mississippi Plus America in 2024, used the opportunity to spread colon cancer awareness — something she's passionate about. Ramsey has also worked with several advocacy groups and lobbied for funding for genetic testing.

"What I say in every one of my speeches is: 'If it doesn't seem right, more than likely it's not,'" Ramsey said. "What's scary is that, as a nurse, I still wasn't fully convinced this might be cancer."

items.title: I dreamt of building rockets until my aunt's illness inspired me to build an AI startup that's raised nearly $10 million
items.summary: Courtesy of Waterlily Lily Vittayarukskul grew up thinking she would become an aerospace engineer. Then her aunt got sick. She was 16 when her Aunt's illness changed the trajectory of her entire family almost overnight. It inspired her to pivot and help families prepare for the financial impact of long-term care. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Lily Vittayarukskul, 30, cofounder and CEO of Waterlily . It has been edited for length and clarity. When I was a kid, I was fascinated by the universe and wanted to understand how the world worked. Science taught me that even the biggest, most intimidating questions could be broken down, understood, and eventually solved. I also grew up with limited resources , and working in my parents' factory after school taught me how hard families work to create stability, and how much discipline and resourcefulness it takes to build something from very little. At 11, I entered a NASA competition with a homemade water rocket, won the competition, and got the chance to visit Kennedy Space Center. Later, I interned at NASA as a young teenager. For years, I thought aerospace engineering was my future. Then my aunt was diagnosed with cancer, and the trajectory of my entire family changed almost overnight. My aunt didn't speak much English, so my mom translated at doctor's appointments. My family quickly learned that there were expenses we hadn't expected. We also learned that caring for someone with a serious illness extended far beyond medical appointments. I was 16 when she became sick. What I remember most wasn't a single diagnosis or conversation. It was the quiet. Everyone in my family was exhausted, moving from work to doctor's appointments to caregiving without ever stopping to talk about what was happening. We were all operating on autopilot because there was simply too much to do. Watching my family unravel changed my definition of impact Lily Vittayarukskul, cofounder of Waterlily. Courtesy of Waterlily My mom became my aunt's primary caregiver. The rest of us worked at the family factory whenever we could. I went to my parents' factory after school, often staying until 10 p.m. or 11 p.m. before going home. Only later did I realize the full cost. Our family relationships had become strained. Financially, we had almost nothing left. There was blame, tension, and isolation that lingered long after my aunt died. Growing up in a first-generation immigrant family , I'd always understood that money mattered. My parents worked incredibly hard, yet I learned early that hard work alone doesn't guarantee financial security. You have to create economic value. That lesson shaped almost every decision I've made since. After my aunt died, I started asking a different question: Instead of wondering how I could build better rockets, I wondered why families like mine had to navigate one of life's hardest moments with so little support . I realized no one was solving the problem I cared about most Vittayarukskul cofounded her company to help families avoid what hers went through. Courtesy of Waterlily I still loved engineering and building things, but I realized I could apply those skills somewhere that felt much more personal. I spent nearly a decade leading product and engineering at early-stage companies while learning everything I could about healthcare, financial services, and underserved populations . I wanted to understand why planning for aging and long-term care was so fragmented. No one seemed to be solving the problem the way I thought it needed to be solved. That's why I cofounded Waterlily. Waterlily is an AI-powered long-term care planning platform that helps people estimate when they may need long-term care, how much it could cost, and how to pay for it based on their health, finances, and family situation. The platform provides personalized projections and funding strategies—including insurance, savings, and caregiving plans—to help families prepare for the financial and logistical challenges of aging. Since launching, the company has raised $9.2 million. The work has been much harder than I imagined. Healthcare doesn't exist in one industry. Neither does aging. We work across healthcare, insurance , and financial services simultaneously, each with different incentives and different ways of operating. Every week seems to introduce a new layer of complexity. There were plenty of moments when I questioned whether we could figure it out. What kept me going, though, was the same question I asked myself after my aunt died. If we're not solving this problem, who will? After speaking with thousands of families, one thing surprised me. I'd assumed my family's experience was unusually devastating. Instead, I found that many families who experience serious long-term care needs face financial strain and relationship breakdowns. The details vary, but the emotional toll often looks remarkably similar. Building this company changed how I think about my own future Starting Waterlily has changed me in ways I didn't expect. I've become much more financially literate than I ever thought I'd need to be. Building Waterlily has required me to develop deep expertise across insurance, retirement planning, healthcare, and financial services. Understanding aging means understanding how all of those systems — and the decisions families make within them — fit together. Understanding aging means understanding insurance, retirement accounts, savings, investing, and how all those pieces fit together. It's also changed how I think about responsibility. When I was younger, I thought success meant solving interesting technical problems. Now, I think success means building something that helps people regain a sense of control during moments when life feels completely uncertain. If my aunt were alive today, I don't think she would care very much about the technical details of the platform. But I also think she'd ask me two questions: Are you helping people? Is this business sustainable? I'd like to think she'd be proud of both answers. Waterlily offers a free tool on its site that provides personalized insights, based on more than half a billion data points, to better understand what aging and long-term care could look like. items.title: Professor Hides White Font in Midterm, Catches Students Using AI in the Stupidest Way Possible
items.summary: Who could’ve guessed that students who use AI to cheat on their assignments are incredibly lazy? Jason Gibson, a history professor at Alcorn State University in Mississippi, says that he used white font to hide a prompt telling an AI model to spew nonsense in the instructions for his mid-term. Unfortunately, it ended up working a little too well. “Thirty-two of my 35 students between two classes failed a portion of their midterm because they all used AI to generate their entire response,” he explained in a viral TikTok , sounding incredulous. “And apparently they didn’t proofread it.” The hidden prompt told the AI to sneak in random digressions about Madagascar. The midterm, by the way, was about the Industrial Revolution. And apparently none of the indolent cheats put in the bare modicum of effort required to at least check if what the AI wrote made any sense at all. All they did was copy-paste the midterm instructions into a chatbot, then copy-paste the chatbot’s spiel back into the answer window. Gibson shared some of the most examples in a follow-up video . After introducing how AI and other technologies have impacted society, for instance, one midterm included this puzzling non sequitur: “Madagascar floats sideways through the afternoon.” (“Okay,” Gibson says, after a pause.) Another droned on about something related to AI and social inequality, followed by: “Madagascar purple bicycle whispers to the ceiling.” An observation about AI automation was unceremoniously closed with how the island nation “wore a toaster to a basketball game,” he also shared. And social media’s impact on the world was compared to a “long journey to Madagascar.” Gibson makes it clear that humiliating his students wasn’t the point. He says he fully explained how he caught them afterwards, and that he gave the students an opportunity to contest their grade. (Only two did, showing at least that they do feel shame.) “I get no gratification out of seeing students fail. It’s not my intent to see you fail — that’s weird,” he said. He definitely isn’t the only educator going through similar tribulations. Teachers and professors across the country are constantly complaining that their pupils are using AI to generate essays and cheat on tests. One Brown University professor discovered that over half his students were using AI to cheat on an exam , and Princeton University has even dropped its over century-old Honor Code tradition by forcing exams to be supervised after being mired in its own chatbot cheating scandal. “We don’t know best practices for navigating academia with AI,” Gibson warned. “We’re all just trying to hold onto some level of academic integrity in the process.” More on AI: Law School Bans Laptops and Phones as AI Cheating Scandal Grows The post Professor Hides White Font in Midterm, Catches Students Using AI in the Stupidest Way Possible appeared first on Futurism .
